This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for controlling a collective of robots via intuitive hand gestures captured by computer vision. We present and assess two distinct methods to decipher the embedded meaning within these gestures for adjusting key parameters of a virtual robot swarm. A comprehensive analysis is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of these algorithms across a range of simulated scenarios, comparing their responsiveness and robustness.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols is the ability to achieve state
evolution within a specific target manifold, regardless of the system's initial
state, even if it's outside the manifold. Our work presents an alternative method
for incorporating the full effects of a non-Abelian geometric phase into the
target manifold state evolution process, presenting two distinct approaches to
this task.

Color images are frequently represented in RGB format and utilized in various image processing tasks. However, grayscale images, another type of representation, are also common and employed in specific applications. Converting between these formats is a common operation in digital image processing, and we have developed an innovative method to achieve this using a cellular automata rule. By converting an RGB triple into a single grayscale value, we can maintain a high level of detail. Additionally, our rule offers other benefits, including the ability to convert between 8 and 15 bit representations and recover lost information with a 1D convolution. We have created a Java implementation of our rule and evaluated it on different types of color images. Furthermore, by representing RGB color components as a point in 3D space, we can analyze our rule's behavior. When mapping the resulting grayscale values back to RGB space, we can obtain an approximation of the original image. We have observed various patterns, including a mapping along RGB component diagonals and areas of uncertainty in the conversion process.

This research paper develops an expression to represent any infinitely differentiable complex-valued function as the sum of exponential functions. Using this representation, we create a discrete version of a function along with its corresponding approximation for the first derivative. We examine the accuracy of these approximations by analyzing the errors involved. The process is then applied to two common numerical challenges: the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and the non-linear advection-diffusion equation.

Given two orientable surfaces S and M equipped with group actions, and assuming the action on S is free while M's action can have fixed points, we investigate the relationship between almost conformal harmonic map instances from S to M under the influence of these group actions and branched covering maps, where the branching points result from the group action itself. When the geometry of M is hyperbolic, we further determine a specific limit on conformal mapping and harmonic mapping characteristics that result from these group actions on S, as expected to be applicable to studying orbifolds with genus zero.

We explore the linear photon-photon collision process to create an electron-positron pair on the path of a plane-wave light wave and explain its occurrence through a novel approach based on underlying quantum principles. The derived formula for this process is a straightforward product of the individual photons' probabilities when they encounter the path of the plane-wave light wave, which is a breakthrough compared to the complicated expression in a standard quantum field theory approach. This breakthrough offers a more intuitive understanding of the linear Breit-Wheeler process, first created in 1931 and a fundamental prediction of quantum electrodynamics, which can be studied in upcoming laser-plasma experiments.

A recent analysis of LHC data at 13 TeV has placed stringent limits on the Two Higgs Doublet Model, with minimum deviation from single-doublet behavior from loop-induced processes. The minimum achievable value for  $\left| m_{12} \right| $ has been found to be around 60-80\text{ GeV} depending on the $m_A$ mass range, with the exception of the CP even case where it is limited by electric dipole moment constraints. Two types of non-decay-type electric dipole constraints have been identified that can satisfy this, with the first being based on electric dipole moment data and the second being based on electric dipole moment data.

We are introducing a relational data exchange framework tailored for RDF data, addressing the constraint that source data is represented as RDF and proposing a solution for enforcing target constraints within this format. The proposed framework leverages typed IRI constructors and RDF graph constraints as the driving force behind RDF data exchange. It also enables the integration of non-RDF target data through relational data exchange mechanisms when necessary. We demonstrate how to define data exchange constraints in any target data type as long as it has a sound mapping to RDF, thereby providing an efficient method for validating data in such types without directly embedding them into the framework. We highlight the effectiveness of the proposed framework by showcasing a range of use cases, encompassing unique features. Notably, our approach yields efficient data loading capabilities into the target data, thereby ensuring that data exchange remains a viable solution in real-world applications, particularly in scenarios involving large datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework tailored for RDF data exchange, leveraging typed IRIs as constructors. This paper presents a range of use cases demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework, with a particular focus on a large-scale scenario where the framework's capabilities are fully realized.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, operations research, statistics and computer science. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now draw upon these techniques, moving beyond traditional nonparametric regression approaches. This paper explores the latest developments in applying shape-constrained regression to economics and operations research problems, with a particular emphasis on recent advancements in the literature over the past five years. It also highlights several areas that require further investigation, including a proposal to expand this analysis further into dynamic systems governed by difference equations.

We suggest a technique for rebuilding particles produced from two massless particles, which can be applied to finding low-mass scalar bosons made of pairs of same-type particles at the LHC. Using simulated data for Higgs bosons produced with photons or particles called Z, our results show the method can give more precise mass measurements and find 68% of all produced particles, which is about the same as the best methods available, but it might be very useful in the future if experiments need even more accuracy.

Pre-trained language models have shown remarkable capabilities in capturing deep semantic relationships and are increasingly being used effectively in syntactic parsing tasks. However, the contributions of these models to syntactic parsing have mainly been described in a theoretical context, with the specific roles of their internal components, such as linear projection matrices in the self-attention mechanism, remaining unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the relationships between these matrices and the constituents of sentences from the perspectives of syntax and sentence structure. We discovered that specific regions within these matrices correspond to distinct relationship patterns, enabling the detection of phrase boundaries and sentence embeddings. Notably, the query matrix, in particular, demonstrates strong correlation with syntactic parsing performance, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

The accuracy of speech-based applications largely depends on high-quality automatic speech recognition systems. This recognition relies on comprehensive training data that accurately models speech patterns. The primary obstacle in developing such systems is access to large amounts of labeled data. Currently, widely used German automatic speech recognition systems rely on the ~100 hours of West German-based COVOST2 corpus. However, these systems fail to account for diverse dialects and accent variations. This research investigates how varying training data sources impact the performance of German automatic speech recognition systems. It specifically focuses on the impact of adding the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus (SWC), which includes data from speakers of low quality and various accents and speech styles, to existing high-quality corpora. The study demonstrates the positive effects of incorporating the SWC and the co-training of West German speech conditions, while also identifying limitations due to resource constraints.

A survey of 2499 Be-type stars, drawn from the LAMOST database, utilized the full-sky survey data of equivalent widths to calculate rotational velocities. A rotatory broadening coefficient was derived from the strengths of the Mg I and Hβ lines, and a range of physical properties, including effective temperatures, gravities, rotational velocities, masses, and ages, were determined using the ATLAS9 models. We discovered that the mean rotational velocity of sampled Be-stars is 171.1±1.3 km/s and decreases with increasing effective temperature. We also observed significant disparities in rotational velocity between split Be-stars and their B-type counterparts. Furthermore, it was found that the distribution of rotational velocities among massive Be-stars exhibits a clear trend, suggesting a gradual decline in rotation speed due to mass loss through stellar winds over time. Our results indicate that the Be-stars' distribution in the HR diagram spans a mass range of 10-28 M$_\odot$ and 4-7 log T$_\odot$, with peak masses and temperatures found in the middle of these distributions. We also found that the peak age of Be-stars is 4.7-6.3 Myr and that the peak masses are found in the middle of the mass distribution. These findings are consistent with theoretical predictions.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is utilized.
Our novel approach, accompanied by an underlying dataset, directly tackles the
accuracy issues associated with existing ITN methods by treating the task as a
supervised learning problem.
Specifically, we employ conditional variational networks to efficiently learn the
transformation from spoken to written language through N consecutive ASR output
vector mappings.
Compared to conventional ITN techniques, our technique achieves a substantial
improvement of 33.6% in terms of accuracy metrics for a large corpus, the TED2000
dataset, under an adequate training regimen.
Furthermore, we identify key components of ITN syntax patterns that are typically
manually incorporated, thereby providing valuable insights for existing ITN
methods and the potential for further accuracy enhancements.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration corresponds to a half-space. Furthermore, using 
spectral analysis, we quantify the rate at which this inequality improves. Our 
research also utilizes the magnetic field to employ the variational method, 
enabling us to address the critical scenario as well.

Deep neural networks, renowned for their superior performance in various tasks, still have a major drawback stemming from their complex design, i.e., their intricate internal workings. This flaw becomes particularly problematic in practical applications, such as medical imaging, where their opaque nature hinders their acceptability. Their susceptibility to malicious attacks and legal issues related to their unpredictable behavior are two specific concerns arising from their inherent opacity. While numerous attempts have been made to address this issue, including the creation of more efficient tools to detect and exploit opaque models, these attempts have not been successful to date.

Our research aims to tackle this challenge by introducing a novel method called DREAM (Difference Equation Attack on Reversible Models), which is the first method capable of revealing neural network designs solely based on their input and output data. Our approach is able to decode even the most complex and well-defended models with just a few carefully selected queries. Our research also demonstrates that traditional model inversion attacks can only recover the weights of a neural network's parameters, not the network's design, and can only succeed with models whose designs are linear in nature. Our method, in contrast, is able to find the exact design of nonlinear models, as well as those with noisy outputs.

Our research presents our attack on various types of neural networks, including those with noisy outputs, linear models, and models with nonlinear designs. Our results show that our approach successfully recovers the design of neural networks in all these scenarios. Our research also presents real-world applications

Despite a well-established method for classifying topological phases in systems with non-Hermitian dynamics and spatial symmetry, the influence of correlations has received less attention. We investigate how correlations impact the topological classification of one-dimensional systems with broken spatial symmetry. By adapting a modified many-body Green's function method, which preserves non-unity eigenvalues, we are able to detect correlation-induced topological phases. Our research demonstrates that correlations can cause phase transitions between different topological phases, including phases with unit eigenvalues. We calculate unit circle crossing points for various correlation strengths in the Ising chain, confirming our results using many-body Green's function spectra. Notably, while one-dimensional systems with spatial symmetry exhibit no correlation-induced topological phases, such phases can occur in systems without spatial symmetry. We relate the observed phenomena to the non-physical nature of certain unit eigenvalues.

Our current research focuses on identifying the characteristics of synthetic speech that contribute to perceived warmth. A proposed hypothesis suggests that acoustic attributes like spectral energy distribution and frequency content convey warmth. We are developing a neural network to evaluate a candidate's performance in generating warm speech. We have created a dataset with human-produced warm and neutral speech samples, and are employing the data to train and assess a neural model. We aim to utilize this model to fine-tune the voice conversion process to produce more warm speech as desired.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_{B-L} symmetries is proposed. It offers realizable mass ranges for dark matter at 1 GeV to 50 GeV and as high as 50 TeV, accounting for both direct and indirect detection constraints. Our findings demonstrate that a radiative seesaw model can satisfy all major experimental dark matter constraints without requiring fine-tuning. The model's intricacy arises from its four Yukawa matrices for fermion singlets, whose masses are determined by the shared minimal dark sector, including a messenger neutrino and superpotential terms involving modular forms.

Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By combining deformed canonical commutation relations with deformed integration measures in the collective shape space, the model is formulated in a way that is invariant under mathematical transformations. As a result, a deformed Schrödinger equation is derived and solved for the harmonic oscillator in the exact ground state. We show that existing deformed potentials can be seen as specific instances in a broader model framework and that key features, like the minimal length parameter, can be calculated in terms of model parameters. Additionally, various properties of the harmonic oscillator are obtained and a specific application to $^{16}$O is made to demonstrate parameter extraction from experimental data. We demonstrate that the model can be used to calculate minimal length in the $^{16}$O nucleus, in addition to its radius, deformation, and vibrational energy.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained attention due to their role in omnidirectional precoding technique. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for odd and even dimensions. Additionally, specific examples are provided to illustrate theoretical bounds and existing lower bounds are improved upon to showcase more efficient Golay complementary arrays.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of processing large numbers of spectral bands within diverse environments. A novel approach involves using a two-stage decision fusion with a highly efficient deep convolutional autoencoder that combines both spatial and spectral constraints. The first stage of fusion integrates the outputs of two autoencoders, one preserving spatial features and another preserving spectral features, allowing for a more accurate detection of changes within remote sensing images. By addressing spatial-spectral redundancy, this method achieves superior results, evidenced by its ability to extract both spatial and spectral features from simulated data, ultimately enabling effective detection of real-world changes.

A molecular fluid's residual entropy is linearly correlated with its viscosity when using the product of its dynamic and reciprocal kinetic energies as a reference, valid across diverse fluid types under varied conditions with an acceptable margin of error.  Our study reveals the underlying cohesion between molecular interactions is preserved in this relation, while incorporating inertial properties alters the slope of the correlation.  A unified equation can effectively predict viscosity in fluids under any condition by calibrating only the molecule's residual entropy and inertia.

The standard model of the cosmological $\Lambda$CDM describes a universe that expands at an accelerating rate and will eventually approach a cosmological event horizon. However, our proposal of a periodic cosmology suggests that the universe's expansion follows a cyclical pattern, characterized by a repeating sequence of phases driven by a novel dark energy framework. Dark energy acts as the driving force behind the expansion and can be mathematically represented by a complex scalar field with periodic behavior in its potential function. As predicted by this model, the dark energy density experiences oscillations as the universe evolves, implying the existence of a cosmological recurrence time. To substantiate the model, a precise theoretical prediction for the cosmological recurrence time and a comprehensive analysis of the dark energy state parameters are presented.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics called the Planck superdeterministic causal model is being proposed. This theory views Bell correlations as the result of massive, shared patterns originating from a very early point in time, specifically the Planck epoch. This shared pattern is encoded within the density matrix which serves as a causal model in a type of classical information theory called block-classicality. This theory offers a new understanding of quantum correlations and presents them as manifestations of highly concentrated, classical correlations across the entire universe, effectively explaining them as 'hard' and 'harder' variants of Bell correlations in a way that aligns with the principle of data processing.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN efficiency by minimizing the size and processing requirements of CNNs for this purpose. To achieve this, we evaluate the performance of a compact CNN (less than 100KB) against other CNNs and Combine with Hint layers to reduce computation load during inference. Additionally, we assess a Clark Wheel approach, which performs initial processing locally and offloads complex tasks to the cloud when necessary.

This study delves into the properties of the two-dimensional Dirac partition function in relation to gauge fields. The partition function's expansion is re-examined within Euler-Mascheroni regularisation, especially for $SL(N)$ gauge fields taking values in the simply connected group. Given that the zero-modes of the Dirac operator exhibit an invariant property under simple root reflections, we derive relations between the values at simple and non-simple roots. Utilising these relationships, we also establish a connection between the values at non-simple and simple roots. Moreover, we derive an expression for the weight lattice using the simply connected group's simply dominant weight lattice. Employing these relationships along with an expression for non-simple Weyl reflection values derived from large mass limits, we develop an algorithm to calculate the Dirac partition function for $A_{n}$ simply connected Lie algebras. Additionally, we derive expressions for $E_8$ and $E_8^{(2)}$ Lie algebras.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly difficult as the number of variables grows, as it typically involves an exponential increase in computational complexity, necessitating both extensive time and financial resources, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. This issue can be resolved by employing a method called the kernel sparse modeling approach, which allows for adapting sparsity-inducing penalties directly in the original data space, thus bypassing exponential complexity scaling. By applying theory from sparse modeling, proven to accelerate processes significantly, researchers have been able to develop novel algorithms, such as the kernel sparse LASSO and support variable selection, which enable sparse models and produce more interpretable results, especially beneficial when paired with kernel support vector machines. This approach has been successfully applied to various high-dimensional, real-world datasets and production environments at Google, resulting in substantial performance improvements and reduced complexity.

In recent years, the use of virtualization in embedded real-time systems has gained significant attention. To meet the growing demand for mixed criticality in embedded systems, the T-Visor project was developed to offer isolated virtualization for such applications. It builds upon the concept of microvirtualization, providing a secure and efficient environment. Our research compares T-Visor against traditional hypervisors and OS-based virtualization approaches, demonstrating its superior performance overhead. The test results reveal that T-Visor offers a secure and efficient virtualization solution for embedded real-time systems.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals often hold their cameras at an angle. In such instances, calculating the camera orientation relative to the scene is crucial for creating panoramic images, especially when capturing multiple images. In this study, however, the camera angle is assumed to be known a priori due to capturing panoramic scenes using specialized devices like GoPro Adapters. Our contribution lies in developing a novel approach to accurately determine the camera angle using only raw panoramic images, including those affected by occlusions. Our approach leverages feature matching and features extracted from the Fourier descriptor to calculate the camera angle relative to the optical axis, even for scenes with multiple cameras, taking advantage of their inherent wide field of view. Our results show promising results in terms of accuracy and robustness, as the estimated camera angle is in line with manually obtained values, and our approach also exhibits strong performance in low-texture scenes, overlapping areas with distortions, and veins present in blood vessel analysis.

We've derived a precise, exact condition that specifies when a network of oscillators with time-delayed coupling exhibits an incoherent yet partially synchronous state known as the frequency-matching pattern in two populations setup. This pattern consists of one population synchronising and another remaining asynchronous. The research focuses on populations of oscillators that follow the simple equation incoherent states frequency-matching pattern incoherent yet partially synchronous state frequency-matching pattern two population synchronisation one fully incoherent, one fully synchronous frequency-matching pattern exact condition frequency-matching pattern exact condition.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust when based on an inaccurate environment model. Our approach involves assessing the difference between the actual and predicted transition probabilities to identify cases where the optimal policy is suboptimal in a data-driven manner, which is significant in model-based Reinforcement Learning. Our experiments demonstrate that adding exploration constraints to model-based Reinforcement Learning algorithms can ensure the policy performs a high proportion of transitions correctly. Our methods effectively work across different model-based Reinforcement Learning algorithms, as shown in our evaluation on box pushing tasks with exploratory actions.

We present a family of infinite-type slice algebras constructed from multi-layer quivers, which encompass previously known examples such as the multi-loop algebra developed by Assem. By utilizing a multi-layer representation of words and combining it with a combinatorial approach to modules, we determine the dimension of the slice algebra over the base field in particular instances.

We've developed a way of calculating reflected entropy in random tensor networks by first determining the optimal contraction network for the entropy product. By focusing on a specific type of graph - the star graph - we've found that optimization often involves an 8-network contraction pattern, leading to a different expression for reflected entropy than the usual max-cut formula. This new expression closely relates to the amount of entanglement within individual edges, highlighting the unique role of reflected entropy in optimizing network contractions. Additionally, our findings reveal that while the type of random distribution influencing individual entanglement entropies has little effect, the Rényi index for the random distribution significantly impacts the reflected entropy calculation. This creates new opportunities for analyzing holographic properties using various distributions, moving beyond traditional i.i.d. and Gaussian models.

Despite its long-standing connection to nonequilibrium thermodynamics, the concept of entropy has proven difficult to quantify in small systems with limited components, with traditional definitions being undermined by ambiguities in intrinsic entropy production rates, robustness against reversibility, and clear interpretation in systems at equilibrium. To address this problem, we establish a new, universal link between non-equilibrium entropy and dissipation, connecting our measure of entropy production in small systems, which we refer to as extrinsic backflow, to thermodynamic entropy in thermal equilibrium. Building upon this link, we derive an equation that successfully unifies disparate findings from non-equilibrium systems, including thermal effects, non-thermal energy, and interactions such as "w w" coupling, into a cohesive framework. To demonstrate the practical significance of our approach, we propose an experimental framework using coupled spin-1/2 systems, which can accurately quantify thermodynamic entropy production in small systems, ultimately enabling predictions about the persistence of coherent patterns in non-equilibrium many-body systems, a phenomenon that could be observed in small systems with intrinsic limitations, including thermal fluctuations and interactions, or in waveguide vector coupling in large systems.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic model of a magnetic reconnection event that takes place when two regions of incompressible, positive fluids collide and are confined within a rigid boundary. As the initial pressure differences grow larger, complex, disordered patterns emerge in specific parts of the fluid's movement dynamics. These disordered patterns accelerate at a rate proportional to the square root of the initial pressure difference. The appearance of chaotic dynamics coincides with two critical points: the onset of supersonic movement and the onset of shock waves in the flow. The development of chaotic dynamics aligns closely with earlier observations of similar systems showing enhanced conductivity when subjected to extremely high supersonic collisions.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that links both scattering amplitudes and classical solutions, as well as suggesting its application to more complex, non-perturbable cases. This review discusses the characteristics of the "kinematic algebra" under the underlying assumptions, and explores whether this model can be adapted to the case of the Wilson loop. The approach taken involves the construction of a non-perturbative model of the adjoint Landau-Lifshitz model on the worldline, and this is then used to outline the gauge theory counterpart, with both versions of the model being embedded within the algebra of the Wilson loop. This, in turn, provides an interpretation of the flat-space double copy limit as the process in which the landau-lifshitz model reduces to the ferromagnetic spin chain. Finally, the connection between the model at hand and other theories that exhibit double copy properties, such as the self-dual Yang-Mills theory and the gravitational theory, is explored.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining the $k$-th moment of hook lengths within partitions of $n$. Our results are based on known observations about hook lengths being divisible by $t$, which show they exhibit a Poisson-like distribution. We derive precise asymptotic estimates for the $k$-th moment of hook lengths as $n$ approaches infinity, utilizing Rogers-Ramanujan identities.

Quantum particles' traversal through barriers has been a long-standing topic of debate due to apparent violations of fundamental principles like the uncertainty principle and causality. In our study, we have devised a unique technique to measure the time it takes a particle to traverse a barrier by employing quantum particles' spin properties during the process. By simulating particles with both mass and spin-1/2 characteristics using the Dirac equation with a rectangular barrier setup, our approach yields results that are experimentally measurable. Moreover, our results demonstrate that spin-precessing particles continuing past a barrier will precess in free space, effectively recording the tunneling time on their spin-precessing path. This approach is not unique to particles with half-spin; similar principles can be applied to higher-spin particles as well using the Dirac equation with the appropriate spin properties.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons. We establish a link between a class of these amplitudes and a universal function. We also identify another type of amplitude that is inherent to each specific meson. Using colour-singlet factorization as a colour correlation between the active quark and antiquum, we derive the leading twist amplitudes' leading order evolution equations. We find that the universal function evolves independently from each meson-specific term, evolving similarly to a scalar meson's leading twist amplitude. We examine various approaches for determining the initial universal function.

Research in quantum interferometry and quantum information processing has greatly benefited from nonlinear quantum mechanics.  However, the conventional method of introducing nonlinearity through a Hamiltonian framework poses limitations when applied to non-Hermitian systems, particularly those operating outside of closed environments.  To address this issue, we propose an extension of the Schrodinger equation that effectively models the nonlinear behavior of open non-Hermitian systems, particularly when subjected to a unitary transformation.  We demonstrate the applicability of this proposed equation in various practical scenarios relevant to quantum technology, including but not limited to phase estimation, compositness breaking, and key distribution.

The extended BMS algebra, derived from asymptotic symmetries of flat spacetime, has a representation in the quantum gravity S-matrix that is also found in the celestial CFT approach.  This leads to a representation of the extended BMS algebra where its representation is 2D given by the superconformal algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(2, \mathbb{R}) \oplus \mathfrak{hs}(2,1)$.  This leads to questions regarding the implications of this algebra's unitarity.

Learning with evolving data and limited storage poses a significant challenge. The task of learning from incremental data without any prior knowledge of the categories is particularly demanding. We have discovered a promising approach based on the concept of sparse memory, which allows systems to recall information after a single exposure. We have proposed a method called Sparse Memory Xor Machine (SXM) for understanding complex category boundaries without perpetually storing information. Our XOR machine utilizes a single layer of interconnected neurons, which can be learned from brief exposure. We have successfully implemented SXM for learning arbitrary 2D patterns with examples only one time and achieved results comparable to other 2D pattern learning methods when considering the amount of stored information.

In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts. By utilizing generalized differential forms with vanishing generalised exterior derivative on a specific type of manifold, one can derive solutions to Einstein's vacuum equations in 5-dimensional metrics. This leads to interesting applications, such as deriving a novel class of geometries with vanishing Ricci tensor and exploring their relationship to Lie derivative symmetries.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over the field $q^q$ for even $q$ published by Pang et. al. [14], this study aims to create new families of permutation polynomials over the field $q^3$ with $q$ being a square, utilizing local parameters.

Despite the existence of effective treatments and vaccines, intestinal parasites still cause significant global health issues and economic losses due to millions of new infections each year. In developing countries, these infections can result in malnutrition, growth and cognitive development delays in young children, while in immunocompromised individuals, they can cause life-threatening conditions. In contrast, North America and Western Europe have seen a substantial decline in human parasitic infections, but the presence of intestinal parasites in pets remains a major concern. This article provides an overview of current research on detecting and diagnosing intestinal parasites in humans and pets, including the use of direct fecal examination, egg counting techniques, and molecular methods. While these methods have different sensitivities and specificities, they all face challenges related to accurate quantification and early detection of infections. In response to these challenges, we suggest potential improvements such as point-of-care testing and molecular point-of-care testing to enhance the accuracy and timeliness of diagnoses. Moreover, we discuss the potential role of artificial intelligence and machine learning in developing more accurate diagnostic tools.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To address these problems, the research adapts a method originally proposed in [17] and further developed in [20]. It involves approximating complex nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDEs using statistical quantities such as the mean and variance. This approach yields an approximated finite-dimensional zero-sum game. It then establishes the error bounds and convergence rate of this finite-dimensional game. Lastly, a numerical example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the method.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and disturbed flight conditions. The mathematical model of the quadcopter is developed in a state-space framework, while a recursive estimator with a Kalman filter estimates the system states, taking into account measurement noise and uncertainty. The proposed controller is designed to regulate quadcopter attitude and ensure robustness, even with uncertainty in the nominal model. By introducing a accelerated term in the control law, this strategy effectively eliminates steady-state tracking errors, outperforming both traditional PID and PID controllers in simulation results, and it has the potential to be applied in intricate nonlinear systems subject to modeling uncertainties and measurement noise.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with an emphasis on quantifying these interactions at the lowest possible energy levels.
Key concepts, including chiral effective field theory, unitarization techniques,
pole extractions, and lattice QCD, are thoroughly discussed and illustrated with practical examples.
A detailed explanation of the partial wave analysis method for solving and understanding
pion-nucleon scattering is presented, followed by an in-depth look at its implementation.
Additionally, a detailed account of the isospin-symmetric and isospin-asymmetric cases
is given, with a focus on its operational procedures. Building upon this knowledge,
the pion-nucleon resonance behavior is explored and, specifically, the N*(1520) $\frac{3}{2}^{-}$
resonance is investigated for extracting its pole position using isospin-asymmetric results.
The results for extracting the pole position in experiments and using chiral effective field theory
in isospin-asymmetric cases demonstrate strong agreement with experiment and lattice QCD.
Furthermore, the results are compared to other extractions, providing evidence for the
 reliability of chiral effective field theory in obtaining the pole position.

A key component of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) tracking system is the silicon pixel detector (SPD), which plays a vital role in detecting high-energy collisions. The upgrade project for the SPD is focused on increasing its interaction layers from three to five. The upgraded detector, set to be installed in 2020-2021, will feature a novel design incorporating double-sided single-layer sensors, a new readout integrated circuit (DSDP-15), and distinct edge bonding techniques for the sensors and readout electronics. To assess the performance and reliability of this new DSDP-15 based design, a prototype module underwent comprehensive tests. The module's performance was thoroughly examined in a laboratory environment and in a simulated CMS detector setup. The results confirm that this design is a successful replacement for the existing SPD.

Our work builds upon the extensive AGN127K sample, a comprehensive dataset comprising 12,700 Active Galactic Nuclei identified within the redshift range $0.07 < z < 0.25$. Leveraging multi-band photometry from Pan-STARRS1, we incorporate new near-infrared PanSTARRS1 $i$-band magnitude and color information to bolster our analysis and select more Active Nuclei at higher redshifts. Additionally, we enhance characterisation of the host galaxies within the AGN sample by employing morphological gradients and classifying the galaxies as either disc, elliptical, or other types. Disc-hosted AGN are predominantly found to be face-on, in alignment with previous findings on starburst galaxies within the same sample.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations within nuclei arise from the short-range correlations (SRC) between pairs of nucleons. These fluctuations are reflected in nuclear density distributions, resulting in a substantial increase in the nucleons' kinetic energy beyond what can be explained by the average mass parameters of the mean-field potential alone. This work presents an in-depth examination of the kinetic energy of nuclei from light to heavy systems, along with its impact on the density distribution and the rms radius. Additionally, the study explores the differences in the kinetic energy of nucleons between neutron-rich nuclei and their symmetric counterparts, and the varying effects of SRC on a specific pair of nucleons.

We are studying complex scaling in neural networks, an approach previously overlooked.
Despite complex numbers' natural extension of real numbers, complex-valued deep
networks remain relatively unexplored. In contrast to complex arithmetic's inherent
stability, its benefits in feature learning are still being investigated.
Our work evaluates complex scaling's utility as a replacement for real-valued
scaling. Combined with a complex version of BatchNorm, this substitution improves
convergence and adds robustness to scale variations. Furthermore, complex scaling
tends to serve as a 'regularizer', enhancing the complex models' accuracy.
The experiments are conducted on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet datasets.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When the gluon distribution approaches a certain limit, a quasi-classical gluon medium emerges, characterized by high energy and a low virtuality.  In this state, the gluon distribution has a characteristic momentum scale - the saturation momentum ($q_S$).  When the total gluon distribution is reduced to the scale of $q_S$, various physical processes occur.  Therefore, the examination of such processes at high energies and momenta can reveal the characteristics of the saturated gluon distribution.  This includes its distribution in both position and momentum space, as well as the correlations between them.

A thorough study examining the abundance of specific chemical elements
within the cores of 42 metal-poor subgiants has been conducted. These elements,
including 10 light elements from sodium to methyl-iron and methyl-barium, were
measured through high-resolution spectroscopy using the HARPS, HARPS-N, and
SPIRUE spectrographs. Moreover, the [X/Fe] chemical element abundance ratios
were compared with values from other studies, revealing internal variability
within each element that ranged between 0.01 and 0.07 dex, suggesting a level of
internal consistency among the elements. Subsequently, a thorough comparison
among the elements and the stellar parameters of these stars was conducted,
revealing no significant variability in their abundance patterns. Consequently,
the internal variability among the elements is estimated to range between 0.06
and 0.1 dex, indicating a level of consistency. Finally, the abundance patterns
were analyzed, and the results suggest that these elements exhibit uniform
abundance trends, excluding sodium and anomalously abundant elements.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed to identify and measure the impact of latent variables on predictive models in large datasets. The proposed framework combines a latent variable machine learning model called LVM, which predicts an outcome using observed variables and a latent variable, with a latent variable occupancy grid map that accounts for conditional latent variable distributions. By leveraging an approximate Bayesian method to sample from occupancy grids, the framework estimates the mean squared error due to latent variables using an explicit latent variable mismatch metric. Through theoretical analysis and an application in a social sciences dataset, the framework demonstrates its usefulness in assessing the impact of latent variables on predictive models.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of various quantum models through a user-defined quantum circuit. SQUID includes a default circuit, which is the hardware-efficient variant with parameterized rotations. As part of the research, the performance of several quantum models has been tested on different datasets, with the Pauling quantum classifier showing the best results, achieving 93% accuracy on the Letter recognition dataset and 78% accuracy on the MNIST dataset.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds. Additionally, we have derived essential conditions for existence semi-slant warped products and gained an understanding of their geometric properties.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop a cost-effective detector with a compact form factor, making it highly suitable for deployment in large-scale event detection arrays at low costs and in small spaces. This technology can be applied to dark matter searches, graviton-photon conversion, and low-energy nuclear recoil detection on various timescales. Its versatility extends to isotope identification for archaeological and geologic research and potentially even exoplanite research. Moreover, pixel-based ionization detectors could operate in extreme environments like deep space and on sub-annual to multi-decadal timescales.

We examine a specific type of active colloid, consisting of two spheres joined together and moving in a environment that isn't uniform in terms of its interactions between the spheres and their surroundings. This study shows that such particles experience a tendency to align or spread out based on the direction of these interactions' driving force. Surprisingly, even particles moving in a environment that disperses or concentrates energy uniformly can display spreading or clustering behavior, as long as the interaction between the spheres isn't completely disregarded. We then develop a reliable method for predicting how this forces affect the alignment between the spheres and go on to accurately model the eventual equilibrium state that this type of colloid reaches. This solution is also applicable to other situations that are more difficult to study.

We investigate various configurations of quasiparticles and quasiparticles in certain fluids at specific densities, such as $
u=1/3$, $
u=2/7$, $
u=2/9$, and near half-filling in a specific theoretical framework that accounts for the effects of finite magnetic fields. Our research reveals distinct patterns and behavior in these fluids, including complex patterns and specific patterns when comparing $
u=2/7$ and $
u=2/9$ to the well-understood $
u=1/3$ case and near half-filling. Our study also reveals the dynamic behavior of these fluids, including their ability to change rapidly or quasi-statically. Our research further reveals that specific patterns and behaviors in these fluids, such as roton minima, can change significantly in response to external magnetic fields and fluid conditions. Our research also sheds new light on the emergence of specific patterns and behaviors in these fluids, such as those seen in $
u=2/5$ and near half-filling. Our research provides a significant step forward in our understanding of these fluids and opens doors to new theoretical and practical applications.

Epidemics spread rapidly through time and both space and social networks. To study outbreaks in a complex contact network, we develop a method to group individuals experiencing similar outbreak trajectories. Our approach facilitates the analysis of epidemic outbreaks in large networks by allowing researchers to study localized epidemics through representative network groups. Using an adaptive clustering technique, we identify groups or clusters of individuals with similar outbreak trajectories and calculate measures to evaluate the accuracy of clustering. Unlike traditional methods that rely on spatial proximity, our method employs dynamic time series to create clusters. We apply our method to a contact network simulation featuring periodic events and observe the formation and evolution of clusters over time. Our results show the effectiveness of our approach in correctly grouping individuals within smaller clusters and correctly identifying the number of clusters. Our method can be used to study localized epidemics in large networks, providing insights into the dynamics of outbreaks.

In the process of transforming distorted observations into clear images, a maximum likelihood estimator is frequently employed, with the assumption that model errors are minimal. However, when preparing data for this approach, various model inaccuracies, such as star formation history uncertainties and instrumental errors, often persist. Our investigation focuses on predicting the magnitude of bias introduced by these preparatory inaccuracies on the estimator, using angular power spectra of simulated data with varying models to assess their effects. Key inaccuracies considered include stellar population uncertainties, instrument errors, and cosmic variance. Our results demonstrate that the estimator is resilient to most inaccuracies, with the exception of star formation history inaccuracies, which can lead to substantial bias, particularly at high frequencies, while inaccuracies in instrument settings can result in a smaller estimated bias.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the ambiguity of terminology, which hinders the teaching learner's understanding. To mitigate this issue, we present a rule-based approach that integrates teaching learner feedback to reduce terminology ambiguities, termed as the act of.fixating. Ambiguity in instructional words, reliant on context for clarification, often confuses the learner and hinders comprehension. For instance, if a teacher describes an object such as 'X' and mentions its characteristics, like 'X has two equal sides', but the term 'X' isn't universally understood, the learner may struggle to grasp the instruction. To address this, the teaching learner can provide feedback, enabling the teacher to clarify 'X' and enhance comprehension. In this paper, we describe.ambiguity, a metric for detecting instructional ambiguities, and develop a strategy for calculating this measure. Building on this foundation, we present the.fixator, an algorithm that utilizes comprehension feedback to eliminate instructional ambiguities through the incorporation of teaching learner feedback. Experimental evaluations across 12 synthesized domains demonstrate that the.ambiguity, when applied to initially ambiguous instructional sets, yields an average ambiguity score of 0.40, which significantly decreases to 0.09 after the.fixator's processing. Additionally, a comparative analysis with human participants indicates that the.fixator effectively refines instructional sets to better align with human expectations, outperforming human adjustments in task completion speed and overall effectiveness.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing a quantum channel's outcomes, it faces an exponential challenge in verifying the reliability of two-qubit gates in light of rising computational needs. To address this, we apply learning and optimization techniques in quantum process tomography. The approach involves two key tasks: the first uses a specific quantum channel limited by parameter constraints to define its boundaries and estimate its characteristics; the second utilizes neural networks to generalize the process for any qubit channel within few shots on a quantum device. Notably, the proposed method achieves process fidelity improvements of 2-3 orders of magnitude compared to previous algorithms. The results demonstrate that using learning techniques can significantly boost the efficiency of quantum process tomography.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great promise for revitalizing communication networks in areas lacking infrastructure, especially when faced with the challenges of high data traffic and limited INFRASTRUCTURE P R O T O C O L S P R O T O C O L S coverage. However, conventional UAV communication systems are plagued by inefficiencies, mainly due to outdated protocols and protocols designed for ground-based networks. To address these issues, a novel UAV communication protocol has been proposed, incorporating a tailored MAC protocol, Prot UAV, that optimizes UAV connectivity, minimizes collisions, and alleviates the dependency on existing ground-based protocols such as IEEE 802.11 DCF. A comprehensive simulation model has been conducted to assess the performance of Prot UAV under varying UAV mobility conditions, traffic load, and antenna gain settings. The results of the simulation reveal that Prot UAV significantly outperforms IEEE 802.11 DCF, showcasing improvements in key metrics including packet delivery ratio, system throughput, average packet delay, and collision probability. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that Prot UAV can maintain high system performance even under extreme UAV mobility scenarios.

The low-energy electronic structure of an aligned bilayer graphene is studied using the vertex renormalization group to understand the effect of short-range interactions. It has been found that these interactions lead to a new type of scattering that enhances low-energy excitations through a continuous relation. The strongest interactions, of charge-neutral type, lead to the emergence of new metallic states characterized by finite momentum related semionic excitations at the Fermi energy. These metallic states display unique properties, such as the absence of Umklapp scattering and linear relationships between parameters. Furthermore, first-principles calculations confirm the theoretical predictions regarding the stability of these metallic states based on the relative positions of certain bands.

A comprehensive analysis of the electronic characteristics and thermal stability of Sc2TbN@C80 and its de-encapsulated, encapsulated, and doped forms was conducted using advanced DFT calculations. Our findings highlight the unusual thermal stability of the endo-encapsulated Sc2TbN cluster, contrasting it with the rapid thermal decomposition of naked metal nitrides. Furthermore, we identified temperature-dependent changes in the molecular orbitals and workfunction of Sc2TbN@C80, which significantly influence its optical properties and potential applications in light-emitting diodes and high-performance organic electronics.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which include various low-powered devices such as sensors and appliances, enabling them to share data over the internet. As these devices are expected to exchange sensitive information, it is crucial for them to be secured. However, standard encryption methods are unsuitable for these low-powered devices due to their high processing demands, which they are incapable of handling. Consequently, there is a need for an advanced cryptographic technique tailored to the requirements of these devices, which they can process efficiently, still ensuring the security of the information they share among themselves or with the central server. This paper presents a novel, lightweight cryptographic protocol specifically designed for the various low-powered devices within the internet of things, which they can use to mutually authenticate and subsequently encrypt their communications over the network.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a primary method to assess the coherence properties of spin qubits, yet its high measurement efficiency makes it unnecessarily costly. To address this, we apply Bayesian analysis to predict Qubit Ramsey measurements, thereby lowering the required number of sequences for a predetermined level of precision in determining the Qubit T2 period. Implementing this technique, we achieve a 4.2-fold enhancement in measurement performance using a single-qubit Ramsey sequence on a Silicon-MOSFET spin qubit, effectively reducing data collection time by approximately 20 hours per T2 dataset.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and its degree. It considers both the Gromov radius and degree when assessing a node's behavior towards being on shortest paths and its neighborhood size. Unlike other metrics, Gromov centrality captures both Gromov radius and degree effects. 

A central property of the Gromov radius is its sensitivity to triangle inequality excess. Experimental results demonstrate a strong correlation between Gromov radius and degree sensitivities to this excess in various network types. Furthermore, a mathematical argument reveals that the triangle inequality excess can introduce bias in centrality results when both Gromov radius and degree increase with it, leading to skewed results by type rather than actual node importance.

To counteract the Gromov radius' effect on centrality results, a measure based on the Gromov radius' sensitivity to the triangle inequality excess is defined and tested within different networks. Results show that, when using the Gromov radius in this manner, other graph centrality metrics' responses to scale changes remain consistent, regardless of the underlying network's degree distribution or triangle inequality excess distribution.

From a purely postulate-based generalization of Newton's theory, our "new" Newtonian theory successfully explains not only the well-established Einsteinian deviation in the Mercury's orbit but also accurately predicts the magnitude of this deviation with remarkable precision. Furthermore, this approach finds a solution to the longstanding Kuiper belt problem by providing support for the existence of the putative planet 9, also known as Planet X. As an added benefit, it is also found that the orbits of both star A and star B in the binary PSR B1913+16, as well as star A in the psr b1257+12 solar system triple, are influenced in a manner consistent with observational findings, thus aligning with the predictions of Einstein's theory of general relativity, but derived from a different theoretical framework. Additionally, it is noted that this "new" Newtonian theory is devoid of non-linear terms, thus eschewing any risk of gravitational wave leakage.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced nearly half a century ago, this concept holds significant application in systems theory and control, where understanding the properties of such bundles remains a critical challenge. In this context, we establish a connection between matrix pencils and Grassmannians of subspaces within a vector space and show that the moduli space of bundles is equivalent to a specific group of transformations. Additionally, we present two key results: a critical inequality and an identity representing an open covering of the space of matrix pencils, representing a major advancement in the study of this subject.

We're investigating the realization of almost abelian solvmanifolds on groupoids under topological T-duality. A key aspect involves a groupoid representation of a universal topological T-duality equivalence related to symplectic leafwise Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms. Additionally, we demonstrate that universal topological T-duality can be represented as a specific Hilbert space contraction within cyclic cohomology.

A recently proposed method enables converting any graph G into a smaller graph G' such that if G' has limited minor-closure properties and a specific transitive relation, then G also exhibits these properties with a specific parameter bound. This conversion also preserves an isomorphism class with a given graph class G. Using this method, when G belongs to the graph class of being H-minor-free and transitivity is preserved, it's discovered that the treewidth of G is bounded by O(MHW^(d)), where MHW is the maximum treewidth of graphs minor equivalent to H within the graph class of G, H is minor-closed, and d is the dimension of the space in which H is embedded. This result improves a previous bound of O(MHW^(2d-1)) by factor 2d.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This is achieved by employing a Lyapunov exponent large deviation analysis for random non-expansive processes, resulting in precise probabilities of random asymptotic convergence to cycles across different initial conditions represented by continuous probability distributions. Furthermore, the probabilities of approaching non-cyclic compact invariant sets, including specific non-cyclic compact convex invariant manifolds and compact convex non-cyclic invariant sets with a positive dimensional interior, are also determined.

The classical simulation of fermionic systems is extremely difficult, but progress has been made in simulating quantum dynamics on classical supercomputers. This is particularly true for fermionic-excitation evolutions which are utilized by many algorithms that target entangled ground states. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of the related qubit-excitation evolutions in quantum simulations. This work builds upon the findings of the previous study, "Fermion-to-qubit mappings produce the most accurate results," by exploring and implementing a variety of qubit-excitation mappings. Notably, the classical computation speed of qubit-excitation evolutions surpasses that of fermionic-excitation evolutions by a factor of ten or more, a speed that is highly advantageous. This speed allows qubit-excitation evolutions to be used to sample from molecular ground-state densities and to solve the Hartree-Fock equations with improved efficiency and accuracy. These improvements are primarily due to smaller numerical errors and faster classical simulation times, but similar effects are expected in variational quantum-fermionic-linear-algorithm-on-qubit-quantum-circuits.

A key challenge in applying variational autoencoders (VAEs) to high-dimensional image reconstruction is the efficient optimization of their complex loss functions. Addressing this issue, our research introduces a Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) that combines a generative adversarial network (GAN) with variational autoencoding to achieve superior image reconstruction. By bypassing the need for an encoder and directly training a compact GAN generator with the discriminator, the DGD achieves a significant reduction in parameter count and computational complexity. This innovative approach leverages the performance of GANs and the regularizing effects of variational autoencoding, resulting in remarkable outcomes in random image completion tasks. Notably, the DGD significantly outperforms standard VAEs with substantially fewer parameters and does not rely on data augmentation, as evidenced by its exceptional performance on high-resolution PhotoReal dataset images.

The analysis of data from Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors has set a maximum limit on the amplitude of the primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background ($\mathcal A_{\rm SGWB}$) with a peak frequency around $100$ Hz, yielding a limit of $0.086$ at $90\%$ confidence. Focusing on the implications for the Universe's early expansion history, research indicates that a peaked SGWB signal could create apparent tension with baryon density constraints from cosmic microwave background observations, specifically requiring $\ln(10^{10}\mbox{ B}/\mbox{H}) > 2.1$. However, the data also shows that the SGWB signal can alleviate the tension between early and late time cosmological datasets. In particular, the analysis finds that the SGWB signal can significantly improve late time datasets, such as the $H_0$ estimation from cosmic microwave background and supernovae observations, reducing the estimation uncertainty from $2.1\%$ to $1.4\%$, while also slightly relaxing the constraint on the $\mbox{H}_0$ parameter from local measurements, allowing for a difference of up to $0.42$ km/s/Mpc. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the late time datasets can be compatible with measurements from cosmic microwave background observations, resulting in a statistically significant improvement in $\chi^2$ values by approximately $\Delta\chi^2 \

The first visit to the inner cometary atmosphere of C/2015 ER61 (ATLAS) on October 18, 2015, has been conducted using the Gemini-South Southern Deep Telescope's optical spectrometer. By utilizing UVVIS's low-resolution spectra, the inner coma was analyzed between the wavelengths of 3200-4600 Angstroms, with a 90 km spatial resolution, specifically within the H$\alpha$-line radius of the nucleus. The nucleus of the comet was discovered approximately 80,000 km from the nucleus, with a spatial scale of 100,000 km. The observed coma contains molecules such as CO, N$_2$, N$_2$H, NH, CH, and possibly C$_2$, with the nucleus being heavily obscured by an obscuring layer. The observed line emissions are broad, with the nucleus being obscured by an estimated velocity of 0.5 Angstroms. The observed emissions are predominantly found at the blue-shifted positions. The observed emissions are found to be consistent with the expected velocity fields of cometary atmospheres. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

In a fractional universe model, observers experience time and space as having a reduced two-dimensional appearance, governed by a modified Walker-Perj\'{e}s action, which incorporates a cosmological constant, fractional cosmological density, and shear. However, this reduced action cannot describe a viable universe when the reduced dimensionality parameter is less than or equal to 1, as this would imply unphysical densities, a negative maximum cosmic density, and instability in the reduced dimensions. Despite these limitations, the model allows for a viable universe with a non-zero reduced dimensionality parameter when assuming a non-zero shear, which also enables solutions resembling de Sitter space, although the reduced dimensions would not be in equilibrium. Furthermore, this modified action does not describe a viable cosmic model when considering a de Sitter space with non-zero reduced dimensions in a flat spacetime, which also fails to describe a stable reduced dimension when reduced to a Schwarzschild black hole, where reduced dimensions would not reach thermal equilibrium, and the reduced dimensions' behavior as an isotropic quantum gas is explored using the specific heat capacity.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems are challenging to optimize due to their complex nature and a vast number of feasible solutions. A novel approach, combining multi-objective branch-and-bound with Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm 2 (NSGA-II), is proposed and applied to a real-world energy optimization problem in building systems. In this approach, NSGA-II initially generates approximate Pareto fronts for continuous and integer variables, which are then used to calculate lower bounds in a multi-objective branch-and-bound tree, using the Normal Boundary Intersection method. A dynamic cutting strategy, leveraging these bounds, ensures efficient node evaluation and elimination. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a hybrid algorithm, BnB-NSGAII, is applied to handle real-world energy optimization problems in building primary energy optimization.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, particularly Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed using the language of simplicial objects within an SDG framework, replacing traditional Hausdorff Lie groupoids with their internal variants. While internal groupoids lack a natural topological structure, they retain conditions for total connectedness, enabling a clear internal definition. Notably, our internal definition aligns with the established classical theory, demonstrating equivalence for total connected Lie groupoids.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding comprehensive workflows in complex cyberinfrastructures, including drones, autonomous vehicles, and medical devices, across the entire system lifecycle. Dynaswap's innovative security model, applicable to diverse domains, ensures robust security even in situations where devices operate independently or are isolated from the main network. This universal model is seamlessly integrated into a dynamic two-layer architecture, comprising a control plane and a device plane, and is complemented by a unique feature - AutoLock. This mechanism automatically isolates untrusted devices from the main network and restricts their functionality to specific sub-components like cameras, thereby preventing unauthorized access and ensuring user control. Dynaswap's cybersecurity architecture also incorporates a unique approach to modeling and verifying the dynamic interactions between control and device planes, and ensures the complete system's safety. Additionally, Dynaswap's cybersecurity framework includes a wide range of features such as role-based access control, robust authentication mechanisms, and secure data transmission with end-to-end encryption. Dynaswap's cybersecurity architecture also includes dynamic data protection mechanisms such as encryption and access control policies, and robust data recovery features to mitigate the consequences of potential failures. Overall, Dynaswap's cybersecurity architecture provides a comprehensive solution to the challenges faced by modern cyberinfrastructures across a wide range of applications and domains.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis is an important task in understanding how people feel about specific aspects in their reviews.  To improve this analysis, researchers have been focusing on modeling the implicit sentiment of aspects that are not directly expressed in words, but are still relevant in the context. A novel approach to tackling this challenge involves a sentiment analysis method called SAMS-IC, which identifies and measures the sentiment of aspects, including those with implicit sentiment. To facilitate further research in this area, a massive dataset of 2.2 million reviews was created by combining the Amazon and Yelp datasets. A substantial portion of the reviews in these datasets contain at least one aspect with implicit sentiment. A pre-trained model called AS-PCABERT, which is specifically designed to identify aspects with implicit sentiment, was proposed. By pre-training the model to perform aspect with implicit sentiment identification and then fine-tuning it for implicit sentiment orientation classification, the model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multiple review domains, and exhibits robust generalization capabilities.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression coefficients and extend this to multi-variable outcomes in linear regression. We establish a link between this approach and coefficients in semiparamolic models for outcome distributions. We extend traditional methods for estimating mediation effects to accommodate binary exposures and outcomes in stratified, case-control studies and provide adjusted formulas for effect decomposition under such designs, which can be implemented using standard weighted logistic regression models without requiring complex post-stratification techniques. We demonstrate the validity of our methods through simulation studies and apply them to analyze data from a study of midlife stress and cognitive decline in women.

This research delves into a secure wireless communication system that incorporates an actively debouncing reflective surface and is powered by a fixed circuit board. The focus of this work is on enhancing the secure data transfer rates of specific users through optimal resource allocation, by adjusting the radio signals and the intelligent reflecting surface's phase shifts. Since the mathematical problem of optimization is complex and non-linear in nature, a new approach is proposed to solve it in two stages. In the first stage, the phase shifts and beamforming vectors are optimized in an iterative manner with the help of some complex mathematical techniques, while ensuring the system remains secure. Next, the resource allocation parameters are adjusted using a more straightforward method to maximize the system's capacity. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, simulation results show that it significantly improves the system's performance compared to traditional methods.

We introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating the capabilities of executive function in few-shot continual learning scenarios. Executive function is conceptualized as the capacity to effectively manage and adapt knowledge gained from previous tasks to successfully complete new tasks with minimal data samples. This framework serves as a unified and adaptable platform for investigating executive function in the context of few-shot continual learning, enabling the assessment of the influence and interactions of multiple learning capabilities on overall performance. By evaluating the combined effects of these capabilities, we can identify their individual contributions, thus facilitating a more in-depth understanding of how a model's learned set of capacities impacts its few-shot continual learning performance.

We have analyzed the solar energy radiation from data collected by the Parker Solar Probe between 2018 and 2021, resulting in an average observation of the solar energy flux normalized to one solar radius as $F_{\odot}= (1.15\pm0.14)\times10^{15}\;{\rm J\;m^{-2}\;s^{-1}}$. The findings are consistent with predictions from Saha's model, however the data revealed significant variations in energy. The distance to the sun at the time of observations, averaging around 28 $R_{\odot}$, was not sufficient to accurately determine a precise lower bound of the energy flux emerging from the sun.

In the context of noncommutative geometry, we explore locally trivial G-C*-algebras. A locally trivial G-C*-algebra can be seen as the sections of a bundle whose fibers are all homomorphic images of the same noncommutative space. We demonstrate that these noncommutative line bundles correspond to a principal G-space bundle with a specific classifying space for the class of such algebras. This discovery allows us to view finite-dimensional noncommutative line bundles as the noncommutative counterparts to vector bundles. By establishing that every G-equivariant symplectic vector bundle has a stable extension which admits a G-invariant metric compatible nearly Kähler structure, we demonstrate that any symplectic noncommutative line bundle can be stably decomposed. This proof relies on key concepts from noncommutative geometry, specifically Morita equivalence and the Stinespring representation theorem, as well as results from representation theory. Additionally, our work demonstrates that any noncommutative line bundle on a compact manifold with dimensions at least 4 has representations of infinite dimensions.
