In optomechanical systems, researchers study $q$-deformed interactions to cause phase transitions and observe the resulting different states. The investigation involves modeling and analyzing the oscillations of magnetization around the system's transition point, which reveals complex and patterned behavior. Moreover, when the system's deformation is not constant, it can still induce phase transitions and create various states, leading to further examination of the dynamics within the system. To understand these dynamics, researchers also analyze the system's stability using two methods. Specifically, they use Landau theory and the spectrum of the Hessian matrix to investigate the $q$-deformed optomechanical system.

In a previous study, I introduced the Two-Rotors Model where any two-mass classical body exhibits two classical scissors modes, featuring two closely spaced eigenfrequencies, one even and one odd under the reflection of classical angular momentum. This theoretical framework has been further developed, covering the case of mass distributions with compact support, and now a new model has been established for mass distributions without compact support. This extension was made using the inverse problem approach, starting from the known two rotors frequency spectrum in Fourier space. However, for general distributions without compact support, there was a lack of corresponding two rotors frequency spectrum in spatial domain. This gap was filled for Gaussian distributions, with the resulting non-local operators being fractional powers of Laplacians, leading to the identification of R-negative scissors modes, with imaginary eigenfrequencies exhibiting odd and even parity.

A new method for solving conservation laws, utilizing cell-average based neural networks, is presented. By utilizing the network's neural numbers to estimate flux derivatives, the method forms an implicit Runge-Kutta scheme. Estimating flux derivatives does not necessitate resolving spatial details, thus enabling the method to employ a network with low resolution. As a result, the method can utilize a larger time step. To validate its effectiveness, numerical experiments were conducted, comparing the method with explicit Runge-Kutta schemes and traditional numerical methods. Results demonstrated significant performance improvements, with results of 1-D Burgers' equation simulations showing results comparable to explicit Runge-Kutta schemes, but with much larger time steps. Additionally, a contraction condition was proposed, which was used to verify results for nonlinear problems. Experiments involving Newton's method were conducted, showing results as good as CN Runge-Kutta schemes. Finally, simulations of conservation laws were conducted in 2-D and 3-D with the results being accurate and efficient, thus verifying the method's great potential for solving conservation laws.

The ALICE experiment has completed its 2022 shutdown to upgrade its ALICE Catcher detector, a calorimeter for tracking heavy particles, to an ability to measure dielectrons with greater precision. In addition, the experiment will install two new detectors to analyze the behavior of quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ionic collisions. The ALICE catchermaker block will be complemented by a new detector to measure the behavior of this plasma in the perpendicular direction to the ALICE axis. The experiment will also be supplemented with a new detector to track the movement of particles within the ALICE axis to improve accuracy in measurements. A new detector will be put in place to track the movement of particles within the ALICE axis to track the movement of particles within the ALICE axis to track the movement of particles within the ALICE axis.

We detail and derive a quantum field theory where the stable vacuum state varies depending on the observer's acceleration, resulting in the well-known Unruh effect. This paper provides a comprehensive framework for investigating the Hawking effect in black holes. By employing a simplified model, we make progress towards understanding black hole evaporation in 2 dimensions. Our focus is on radial null geodesics, yielding insights into the formation of a horizon and the resulting thermal radiation characteristic of a black hole.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves identifying event instances, which comprises detecting event triggers and subsequent event arguments. This paper presents an innovative unsupored and supervised approach to argument extraction, drawing inspiration from human thought processes. Furthermore, we establish two distinct methods for extracting arguments utilizing existing trigger annotations. These methods are evaluated across six different datasets under both and not only under supervised conditions but also with varying levels of success in unsupored settings, demonstrating our model's superior performance in argument extraction.

We examine a complex manifold with a holomorphic line bundle and a positive $(1,1)$-form $\omega$. Assuming that the top-degree wedge product of the exterior differential with $\omega$ is a constant, multiple power forms of $\omega$ are proven to be exact under certain conditions, specifically when $p > q$, $p+q=p_0(\omega)$, or $p+q=p_0(\omega)-1$, where $p_0(\omega)$ is defined as the order of the positive Lefschetz thrashing of $\omega$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula in the case where $p+q=p_0(\omega)-1$, akin to the Jacobi-Trudi identity.

The impact of a steller wind on the accumulation of material in a high mass X-ray binary's accretion disk has been examined. Observations of the accretion disk dynamics in the source Cygnus X-1, which exhibits distinct time-scale and amplitude changes in its X-ray emissions, suggest that the effect of a stellar wind has an influence on its behavior. Simulations using the Fokker-Planck equation model the accumulation and dissipation of the accretion disk in response to the binary's boundary conditions, including its mass loss due to a stellar wind. Results indicate that the presence of a stellar wind significantly affects the power spectral density, especially for low-frequency oscillations, with the density fluctuating inversely in proportion to the width of the accretion disk, a trend that is also evident in the disk's radius and mean density. These findings align with previous studies on normal high mass X-ray binaries, with a notable difference being that sources exhibiting stronger winds show a greater discrepancy between the measured and predicted power spectral density, a phenomenon also observed in X-ray binaries, including Her X-1, 4U 0115+6J, 4U 1735-44, and V404 Cyg, suggesting that the effect of a stellar wind has a notable impact on the behavior of these sources.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically focusing on their quantization and renormalization within the context of Smolin's non-abelian aether-like term.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing, despite task-specific models excelling in their respective areas. Contrary to a 2019 study suggesting joint learning yields little improvement, our experiment reveals single-task models to be equivalent or even inferior to their multi-task counterparts. By expanding joint learning to cover more data and text types, we find joint models to outperform separate models in parsing both syntax and semantics. When added to state-of-the-art systems, we find joint models bring the benefits of increased data without compromising individual tasks' performance. Additionally, we observe joint models to be particularly effective on low-resource datasets, both linguistically or domain-based.

The relationship between a black hole's spin and the mass ejected during the merger has been explored using a set of highly accurate models. Our investigation reveals that for a specific measure of spin, called the final mass spin, the relationship between the mass ejected and this spin parameter follows a consistent pattern across a range of the spin parameter. This discovery suggests an alternative way to express the spin parameter that better captures how the mass ejected affects black hole spins. This new way of defining spin, based on the mass ejected, aligns with an alternative proposal that links each spin to a fraction of the mass ejected. This relationship also matches our understanding of the individual spin spins using existing models or by treating them as test particles moving around the final black hole. This comparison provides insight into the behavior of the remnant spindown and offers a testable prediction for gravitational wave observations.

We have carried out an in-depth investigation into tidal features within the Dracones and Virgo North galaxy groups. Utilizing data from the DEVCAL survey and the Zwicky Vacuum Telescope, the Dracones galaxy group was observed with high-resolution data, data with a wider field of view, and Hubble Space Telescope data. We discovered that a significant portion of massive early-type galaxies in the Dracones and Virgo North galaxy groups are associated with prominent tidal features. Specifically, around 20% of these galaxies are found to have a distinct tidal component with a contribution of more than 1% of their total flux. Furthermore, when including galaxies with a less distinct tidal component, this figure increases to around 50%. We also observed that the majority of these galaxies exhibit a tidal component with an apparent size of more than 10 kpc. These findings are comparable to those found in other large galaxy surveys. We have also identified a notable number of galaxies within the Dracones galaxy cluster that are likely the result of past mergers. Furthermore, our study suggests the presence of a higher density of tidal features within the Virgo cluster's vicinity.

This paper is a component of a series on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which incorporates an asymmetric gravitational effect, akin to the electric field in polar regions, with a potential repulsive component. We investigate this effect in compact bodies, such as stars, by examining their mass distributions and gravitational interactions. We employ a model-based approach to study these systems, focusing on the distribution of their mass and the resulting metrics, while ensuring pressure stability and causality. We examine two distinct scenarios, introducing a model for the interaction between the system and this parameter, which enables us to calculate the system's total mass. We then assess these results by comparing them to standard scenarios and through numerical analysis, examining the influence of this parameter on unique properties, such as repulsive gravity and unique metrics. We assess the consistency of this research with astrophysical observations, such as star mass limits and neutron star mass limits, as well as observations of binary pulsars.

Optical observations of fast radio bursts (FRBs) are particularly suitable to unravel their underlying origins. Despite notable attempts, no optical counterparts to recurrent FRBs have been pinpointed, casting doubt on many hypothesized sources. By utilizing the Euclid satellite's wide fields of view and swift redistribution of trigger lists among a clustered network of telescopes, we can execute highly targeted and timely follow-up observations. This paired system, designed to be part of the Euclid collaboration, will enable the detection of faint optical transients, even those with extremely low repetition rates. By expanding the Euclid ECAL's scientific output to include highly dispersed transients, we can greatly enhance our comprehension of the universe's most explosive events. Moreover, the MicroMaTeR project, aimed at identifying the cosmic origins of gamma-ray bursts, neutrino sources, and gravitational waves, will greatly increase the former's capabilities to include FRB detection, yielding valuable large-scale structure information through axial repetition timing analysis.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, medicine, industry, photography, and power supply. The latest research in this field has primarily centered on optimizing existing technologies or exploring novel phenomena to achieve further breakthroughs. The integration of high-power, ultrashort lasers with cutting-edge nano/ultra/ultra-small processing methods has the potential to revolutionize multiple fields, including electronics, semiconductor, nanotechnology, and biophotonics. The ultimate goal is to establish a unified, high-power, ultrashort ultra-advanced optical laser station that can efficiently utilize its capabilities. Multimodal AI applications have shown significant potential in addressing real-world challenges. However, existing methods for image-text tasks are often limited, requiring either extensive modifications to the input or limited generation capabilities without an associated input image. To address these limitations, we introduce the MAGIC framework, which enables high-quality text generation directly from the input image without any additional prompts. We achieve this through a combination of techniques including a high-level guide that specifies the text's semantic content and a low-level guide that ensures alignment with the image's visual details. We successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of MAGIC in a range of image-text generation tasks, including image captioning, art captioning, and reverse captioning.

We present DRCT, a delegated RingCT signature scheme, and its decentralized
variant, to bolster the security of confidential cryptocurrencies. DRCT enables
cryptocurrencies to maintain unbreakable transaction privacy, integrity, and money
supply control. Although existing decentralized versions in the literature offer only
a limited form of trust-worthy anonymous transactions, DRCT fulfills a higher
standard of unimpeachable security, followed by the development of delegated and
decentralized versions of the DRCT scheme. In addition, we compare our security
model with the existing decentralized RingCT schemes to showcase its superiority.

In 2015, the LHCb experiment at the CERN LHC conducted multiple emittance scans, resulting in a detailed understanding of the dynamic range, which revealed the presence of two major oscillation modes, and an finer set of smaller oscillations. Although these oscillations aligned with the expected dynamic range, their finer modes did not match the predictions from the standard acceleration model. Additionally, we analyzed the correlations between the protons, which indicated a weak horizontal-vertical correlation, contradicting the expectations based on the standard acceleration model. A comparison with a simplified model, incorporating only the primary observed frequencies, was conducted, which indicated that this simpler model could not account for the complexity of the observed motion.

In artificial neural networks, a significant issue known as catastrophic forgetting hampers the capability of continual learning. Studies have shown that deep networks with gradient-based fine-tuning tend to significantly compromise their ability to retain previously learned tasks, even after just one adjustment cycle. Prior research has proposed solutions such as elastic weight freezing and plasticity normalization, however these methods encounter challenges when it comes to ensuring a consistent level of performance across multiple architectures and training scenarios. We introduce a new technique, dubbed Consistent Learning Rate Scaling, ConsLS, that aims to tackle this problem by scaling the learning rate for individual network weights in a way that minimizes the impact on older tasks while still achieving good performance on new tasks, effectively fine-tuning the learning rate to find the optimal balance between remembering old tasks and understanding new ones. Our approach involves adding an additional constraint to the consistent learning rate problem, which forces the model to stay close to its previous configuration, and scaling the learning rate accordingly. We show that ConsLS significantly outperforms its state-of-the-art competitors on a wide variety of tasks, including image classification, speech recognition, and language processing, and does so with much less additional computation than state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, ConsLS is highly effective at achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark tasks, and does so with the flexibility to work with different model architectures and training datasets.

This research presents the initial observation of two decay pathways, specifically $\Upsilon(10753) \to \Upsilon(nS) \pi \pi$ with $n=1$ and $2$, accompanied by their branching ratios. For the decays $\Upsilon(10753) \to \Upsilon(1S) \pi \pi$ and $\Upsilon(10753) \to \Upsilon(2S) \pi \pi$, their respective branching ratios were determined to be $(29.9 \pm 5.5 \pm 3.9)\%$ and $(11.0 \pm 2.0 \pm 1.0)\%$, taking into account the statistical and systematic uncertainties. These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that these decay processes are predominantly one-gluon exchange transitions.

In recent years, deep learning has experienced significant success in various applications, but its adoption is hindered by its high computational demands. To address these concerns, researchers have been exploring quantized neural networks that utilize low-precision weights, enabling efficient deployment on edge devices. This paper presents an innovative approach, referred to as IQPNE, which employs the principle of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust neural network quantization. As entry points into a quantum circuit change based on the input data's one-hot encoding, varying quantization levels can be achieved without pre-design. Experimental results demonstrate IQPNE's superior performance over existing methods in terms of both accuracy and model training efficiency.

The intrinsic robot's flexibility and the soft material's inherent nonlinearity pose significant control difficulties, including the complex 2D or 3D shape and the material's non-linear properties. However, the use of soft robotics in real-world applications, such as interacting with objects and humans, is made more feasible by addressing the intrinsic challenges. In this research, we present a method for accurately modeling and controlling a soft robot arm through the integration of a machine learning approach. Specifically, we utilize a neural network trained on a finite element analysis of a flexible robot made of muscle-like material to simulate its behavior under actuation. Additionally, we take into account the impact of gravity and external noise on the model, providing a grounded, accurate, and efficient model for use in various control strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that the model-based controller significantly outperforms a controller without model knowledge and is competitive with a controller that counteracts environmental noise.

Verifying facts using structured data requires matching and comparing data in a precise, machine-readable format that adheres to strict evaluation and evaluation result rules. Despite the established importance of this task, current AI-driven methods are mostly designed to extract necessary information without considering it, leading to significant computational inefficiencies when comparing large datasets. Our proposed approach addresses these shortcomings by developing a modular, task-specific algorithm that leverages structure-aware representation learning to achieve efficient data comparison. Our experiments on a standard benchmark show that by utilizing structure-aware representations, we can substantially reduce the computational cost, achieving comparable performance to current state-of-the-art models at the expense of only a minimal decline in accuracy.

The field of deep generative models has made significant strides in creating realistic synthetic imagery without the need for labels. Nonetheless, models that rely on unsupervised learning often fall short in terms of producing high-quality synthetic data that accurately reflects real-world objects. On the other hand, supervised methods tend to generate imagery that is more accurate and of higher quality on average. This has led researchers to explore a potential compromise by using unsupervised learning to identify meaningful object categories within an existing dataset and then generating targeted synthetic images. By adopting this approach, it is possible to create images that are categorized according to predefined object classes. Our proposed method combines unsupervised learning with the power of the StyleGAN2 generator to generate high-quality synthetic images. Our strategy involves using the unsupervised object detection algorithm, Detectron2's X-Net, to categorize the objects in an existing dataset and solving the resulting classification problem through a mapping of the unsupervised cluster to the generated space. Our method has demonstrated notable improvements in both the accuracy and the quality of the synthetic images it produces.

A new method has been developed to perform Bayesian inference in complex, multi-parameter problems by combining Bayesian inference with Bayesian deep learning. This technique creates a deep neural network that maps from the parameters of a complex statistical model to its posterior distribution. The design of the neural network is guided by a heuristic method, called differential evolution, which effectively explores the parameter space even in high-dimensional problems. This method was tested on a range of statistical tasks, including those with and without a clear hypothesis, and outperformed other state-of-the-art methods in several of these tests. Notably, it was able to efficiently process large datasets, even with up to a hundred thousand observations.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network. When two non-malicious points $u$ and $v$ are connected by a fault, and a third point $w$ exists, the label of $v$ should reflect the shortest distance between $u$ and $w$ through $v$, even if that fault is present. We've established that any fault-based labelling system must have a minimum description length of $\varOmega(\log_2 n)$, where $n$ represents the number of points. Furthermore, we have developed a new method, known as multiplicative labels, that can accurately calculate shortest distances between any pair of non-malicious points, given a set of edge weights, by using an approach inspired by efficient algorithms. Our study shows that in sparse networks, each point can be labelled with a length of $O(\log^2 n)$, whereas in dense networks, each point can be labelled with a length of $O(\log n\log n)$. Our work is unique in that it doesn't assume any restrictions on the network's structure or the nature of its edge weights.

In this research, we studied two-particle correlations in systems of bosons and fermions using a non-equilibrium quench scenario that transitions from a random Fock state to a situation of complete interactions in the absence of further interactions. We found that for both bosons and fermions at half filling, two-particle correlations display significant and regular oscillations at mid-range distances. The frequencies of these oscillations are determined by the imaginary component of the Liouvillian gap. Furthermore, we observed the development of long-range order at half filling in both particle types, resulting in a phase described by the Ising model. The order in boson systems was achieved through the development of a non-zero magnetization, whereas in fermion systems, it manifested as the emergence of a fermion density wave.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$ and a source term $f$, we establish the existence of a unique weak solution in the context where the equation is subject to a given initial condition represented by a function $g$ on the boundary of the domain $\Omega$. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of weak solutions when the coefficient $A$ satisfies a bounded condition and the domain $\Omega$ is in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n$ is an integer greater than or equal to $2$. Moreover, we show that the solution also satisfies a uniqueness condition when the coefficient $A$ satisfies a stricter ellipticity condition and the domain is bounded. Our findings are further supported by an illustrative example in which the coefficient $A$ does not satisfy the stricter condition and the domain is unbounded, thus failing to guarantee the existence of weak solutions under the specified circumstances.

To address the challenge of non-representative training data in medical image analysis tasks, out-of-distribution detection is becoming increasingly significant. Given the labor-intensive nature of medical image acquisition and expert annotation, developing an efficient data distribution approach is critical. Our proposed solution utilizes a contrastive learning framework that trains distinct encoder networks for model data and real test data, which can accurately distinguish between them. By generating contrastive learning pairs using only existing model data, as annotation is resource-intensive, we establish a robust representation of the model's data distribution. Our extensive experiments across multiple datasets validate the efficacy of our approach in identifying out-of-distribution samples.

In a driven open quantum system coupled to a thermal bath at a certain temperature, the system reaches a nonequilibrium steady state, which no longer depends on time. Our research examines how this steady state evolves as control parameters are modified. It is found that when the driving force is gradually increased, the steady state undergoes sudden changes in its populations at specific thresholds - the quantum nonequilibrium phase transitions (QNPTs). These transitions can be understood through an adiabatic approximation applied to the thermalized steady state of the driven system. Our findings demonstrate that this approximation can accurately predict the locations and nature of QNPTs in a variety of quantum systems, including a two-level atom, a three-level atom, and a qubit, under different conditions such as temperature and coupling. The application of this method opens up new possibilities for studying the effects of thermalization on quantum many-body systems and developing novel quantum technologies.

The investigation leads to an Alexandrov maximum principle for convex functions with zero boundary conditions. Additionally, it is shown that p-harmonic functions on p-minimal surfaces are Holder continuous. Moreover, the Holder exponent for p-harmonic functions is proven to be at least $\min\{1, \frac{2}{p}\}$ for $p > 2$ and $\frac{2}{p}$ for $p \in (1, 2]$.

Counting the random events occurring over a specific period can lead to the creation of accurate time-measuring tools, which, in principle, are achievable as long as there's a reliable frequency source for the clock's frequency reference. This class of quantum time-measuring devices includes not only the commonly used atomic and photon counting clocks but also a broader category of quantum clocks. These newly considered quantum clocks utilize quantum systems that cycle through distinct, interacted quantum states, producing random events. Because stochastic processes are involved, new design aspects and time-keeping limitations have emerged, which we will discuss in detail. This paper also delves into the underlying mathematics of quantum time-keeping devices, which we believe could have broader applications beyond quantum clocks.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) and explores their relationship with Fog computing and the Content Centric Networks (CCN) architecture. The study's primary objectives are Fog architecture integration, application optimization, and the efficient allocation of application instances to reduce latency, while also addressing security and multi-criteria issues such as energy consumption, bandwidth utilization, and Quality of Experience (QoE). The work's essential component is the development of an optimal, latency-minimizing architecture, along with an expert system that can provide tailored solutions for application optimization based on user-defined constraints. The Fog-SDN platform's implementation and the typical latency times associated with Fog computing are discussed, with an emphasis on the challenges presented by Fog computing and the research tools presented to address these issues.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss method is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. When combined with data augmentation, this goal can be achieved more efficiently. However, traditional pair-wise loss approaches require extensive computations to calculate losses for all class augmented pairs. To counteract this limitation, we introduce Fast Loss Mining, a technique to accelerate the calculation of pair-wise loss by significantly reducing the number of mined pairs. Experimental results indicate that Fast Loss Mining yields state-of-the-art performance on the Cars3 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks with substantially faster training speeds compared to existing methods.

We investigate various holographic tensor networks with an emphasis on those that exhibit special capabilities for quantum error correction. This class of networks, including various forms like PEPS and tensor product states, possesses notable characteristics such as bond dimension limits, entropic inequalities, and specific entanglement patterns. These properties become increasingly prominent as we limit the allowed errors, particularly those involving split subspaces. This distinct entanglement structure inspired by holography sets these networks apart, enabling various applications in quantum computing and facilitating an in-depth study of their resilience against general and correlated noise.

Recent findings have revealed a peculiar set of magnetized radio filaments in the center of the sky that exhibit a clear grouping pattern along with other unique characteristics such as polarizations, intensities, and shapes. To better understand these phenomena, researchers conducted a thorough examination of one notable group containing five filaments, revealing intricate thread-like structures below the original resolution. An in-depth analysis of these threads' physical and magnetic attributes, including their 3D shapes and thread diameters, was performed. Furthermore, scientists explored the relationship between the described group and neighboring similar entities. Results indicated that the observed set is not isolated in its properties but rather integrated with other entities in the same region. Based on these observations, researchers suggest that these magnetized radio filaments are likely related to processes such as magnetic reconnection and possibly part of a larger entity like a giant arc structure, although further investigation is required.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing the voltage increase and reduced power factor, especially during grid failures with zero voltage and power from renewable resources or grid interruptions.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and history. The vast array of algorithms existing in a full information setting are rendered ineffective when faced with time-independent delays, having all been proven to be ineffective for such delays. In contrast, our proposed algorithm is perfectly suited for dealing with time-dependent delays, having been developed in response to Li's query on adapting regret-minimizing algorithms to this setting. By leveraging the concept of time-anticipating times in causal intervals, our algorithm strikes a delicate balance between exploration and computation complexity, which is heavily influenced by the delay causality. Specifically, we demonstrate the feasibility of an exploration strategy that leverages computation. Consequently, we establish that our algorithm is the first algorithm to be feasible in all causal delays with delayed feedback, thus achieving the best possible regret of $O(T^{7/8})$ within a time horizon of $T$. Furthermore, our results are not restricted to the full information setting, but can also be applied to the limited information setting.

Recent advances in task-oriented dialogue have led to highly effective, rational learning models, yet these advancements often come at a cost - the tendency for these models to over-learn specific phrasing, thereby hindering their ability to adapt to new situations. To address this issue, our research introduces an innovative, regularized learning method that enhances lexical versatility by leveraging "nearby" states, which are similar due to using synonyms, in guiding policy decisions. By regularizing towards these similar states, our model achieves smoother transitions between dialogue actions, and as a result, it exhibits improved dialogue diversity in various scenarios. Additionally, theoretical backing and comprehensive testing on a dialogue management dataset confirm the efficacy of this method, demonstrating its ability to boost lexical versatility without compromising overall dialogue performance.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization approach occurred with Kenneth Wilson's formulation, enabling a line of research investigated primarily in non-perturbative contexts. One such line of research involved the lattice formulation, which facilitated the quantum chromodynamics' numerical examination of non-perturbative properties. The lattice regularization provided a discrete, finite number of degrees of freedom system, analyzed through the Monte Carlo method under specific conditions. This contribution focuses on the history of the lattice formulation up to its current status in research, specifically highlighting the challenges and solutions regarding the mass term in the lattice regularization.

A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points is proposed for predicting the loading conditions on offshore wind turbines during extreme storms. The variability in response to identical storm events is known as heteroscedasticity, and it can be accurately modeled to reflect the uncertainty in actual loading conditions. The variability in loading patterns is due to the stochastic nature of wind speed time series, which varies from one realization to another. The main challenge in working with Gaussian process regression when dealing with multi-dimensional output data lies in the rapidly increasing computational complexity. To overcome this limitation, a sparse GP regression technique, known as the Conditional Latent Function GP, is adapted to address the high-dimensional nature of covariance functions. By leveraging the strong correlations in time series data, this method achieves significant computational savings by reducing the computational cost to a more manageable level. The sparse GP regression approach is then applied to predict the turbulent wind speed time series and torque torques experienced by a 5-MW offshore wind turbine.

Turkey experienced a devastating 7.8 magnitude earthquake in southern regions on February 6th, 2023, resulting in thousands of casualties. Prior to this event, another earthquake of the same magnitude struck the same area on February 4th, 2023. Researchers initially investigated how citizens reacted to these disasters on Twitter by analyzing their posts within 24 hours. Their analysis involved examining citizens' posts related to public relations, rather than just location and syntax, utilizing a frequency analysis. Following this, they developed a Twitter account monitoring application to track various aspects, including public relations and syntax. The research culminated in a dataset containing 4,271 posts, used to train and refine machine learning models. By employing preprocessing and feature extraction, the models were trained to classify posts based on intent, resulting in 80.57% average test accuracy. The developed system was subsequently deployed on specific websites to provide real-time, automated, and dynamic content for relevant parties.

We re-examine the property R#subscriptall introduced by Borel and Serre, which originally stated that an infinite group with property R#subscriptall has only one twisted conjugacy class. It turns out, however, that in the context of minimal asymptotic cones, the original property should be modified to focus on the triviality of all non-classical twisted conjugacy classes. The revised concept is formally introduced, accompanied by an associated definition of property R#subscriptall*. We further demonstrate that this revised concept holds for our previously defined noncommutative spaces具有finite cohomological dimension.

A novel technique for reconstructing time-evolving velocity fields from a known flow history up to a future point is developed. This technique employs a stability factor that builds upon the Taylor expansion of velocities and ensures the continuity of velocities. By leveraging this approach, we demonstrate the existence and stability of the inverse problem's solution within the Laplace domain and achieve stability in the time domain through the use of the Z-transform. This technique is then applied to the deconvolution of the nonlinear advection equation and extended to the inversion of the Navier-Stokes equations using previously derived decomposition equations. In a grid-based simulation, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms other inversion methods in terms of accuracy when estimating time-resolved velocity fields from their time-integrated counterparts.

This paper introduces the Scented Naturalistic Driving Dataset (SceNDD), a comprehensive driving data collection designed for semantickick scenario generation. The dataset features six primary data channels - a 1080p video feed, steering angle, pedal positions, GPS location, and flight path video - and includes detailed visual annotations. A total of 124 hours of driver data and 1122334 driving segments are captured from two drivers in various weather and lighting conditions. The dataset also includes a user-friendly visual editor, enabling segment exchange and task-specific filtering.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this emerging field, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT. Starting with BCFT's reflection, we derived a way to define reflected entropy in boundary theories, particularly BCFT and BCET. When working with pure AdS$_3$ spacetimes using HRT formula, our approach allows us to relate reflected entropy to the entanglement wedge cross section's area. Additionally, from universal formulas for ReAdS$_3$ spacetimes, we calculated reflected entropy for universal CFTs and one-dimensional systems under specific conditions. Furthermore, from information theory, we showed that certain information quantities in ICFT are equivalent to others in established CFT theory.

We explore the use of reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) to enhance the capabilities of orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems, providing both enhanced coverage and a larger service area. To optimize the these systems, we develop a multi-objective approach that aims to increase the number of served users at a specific data rate threshold, along with the overall data throughput. This optimization problem is constrained by the RIS' power and peak power capabilities and the available bandwidth for OFDM. By transforming the problem into a single objective function and employing the successive convex approximation method, we achieve a faster convergence rate. To further increase the efficiency, we convert the non-convex power constraints into linear inequalities by applying the geometric average arithmetic average inequality, resulting in a convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using the interior point method. To effectively achieve the optimal power distribution, we break down the combined power into per-frequency components, thus reducing the dimensionality and simplifying the optimization process. Our approach benefits from the low peak-to-average power ratio of OFDM signals and the ability to implement individual RIS power levels across frequency subcarriers. We provide two implementation strategies for the RF and analog circuits, analyzing their impacts on the system's energy efficiency and convergence speed. Our results show that the proposed power distribution method outperforms existing solutions under various scenarios, particularly when the available power increases, leading to a faster convergence rate and lower computational complexity.

The theoretical framework for globally optimal local meter configurations that achieve this purpose has been established by researchers in this field. Furthermore, an investigation has been conducted to assess how various meter quantities are susceptible to the constraints imposed by the principles of quantum mechanics. It has been discovered that a crucial factor influencing an local meter's ability to accurately and optimally capture an energy value is not its precision per se, but rather the extent to which the superposition of potential measurement outcomes is present within its spectrum. This finding has been verified through an in-depth case study of a quantum harmonic oscillator's energy measurement process.

We have established a connection between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, as well as between integrally almost Hermitian structures and real Killing spinors. Additionally, our research focuses on obtaining lower bounds for the volumes of almost Hermitian manifolds with integrally biholomorphic Killing spinors and for nearly Koehler manifolds with Killing spinors. Specifically, our volume estimates show that the volumes of such manifolds with flat torsion cannot be arbitrarily scaled down. The existence of such Killing spinors also imposes restrictions on the almost complex structure, leading to a requirement that the almost Hermitian manifold be formal. The paper concludes with an examination of whether non-compact examples exist and shows that the flat torus is the only known compact example.

The global spread of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 has led to an unprecedented pandemic, prompting the development of contact tracing apps to contain its spread. However, these apps raise serious privacy concerns, as they have the potential to infringe upon the privacy of individuals, even when accompanied by privacy safeguards. Our research focuses on SCOVID, a contact tracing app that employs Bluetooth technology and aims to inform users of potential COVID-19 exposure. A real-world study was conducted to assess the privacy risks associated with the data collected by SCOVID, using synthetic and real-world information. Our findings reveal that the SCOVID data allows for the inference of users' health status, group affiliations, and locations, thus exposing them to the potential of re-identification.

The main goal of this research is to delve into the connection between uncertainty principles and fundamental features of quantum mechanics, including superposition, entanglement, and self-interference. We demonstrate that the randomness seen in measurement results is due to nonlocal correlations resulting from the superposition state and self-interference of the wave function. Additionally, our findings reveal that bipartite entanglement is responsible for local correlations in classical measurement outcomes, while multipartite entanglement influences multipartite local correlations. Ultimately, our analysis provides a unified understanding of various quantum phenomena by emphasizing the crucial role of entanglement.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected by a three-body resonance relationship has recently been discovered. Researchers have conducted a comprehensive study using the Namunuu integrator to analyze the dynamics of five specific asteroids within this cluster. By applying this analysis to four members of the cluster, a significant finding emerged: a chain of mean motion resonances involving a 1:1:1:1:2 ratio, which effectively captures the cluster members' orbital configurations. Additionally, researchers have integrated the Namunuu findings with a network-based approach to identify more compact members of the cluster, while also providing new insights into the cluster's configuration and member connections.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is achieved by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in the 2018 Communications in Number Theory and Algebra paper, and utilizing a generalization of Atiyah-Bott's topological recursion series based on elliptic cohomology.

Recent advances in making algebraic geometry more accessible through computerization have led to significant development in computational methods, particularly in using symbolic techniques to address complex geometric problems. As a result, researchers have started exploring the potential of using machine learning, a typically algebraic-geometric approach, to solve problems in algebraic geometry. Although this innovative approach is relatively new, machine learning's application to algebraic geometry has shown promise in areas such as topology and geometry, specifically in decoding codimension one cycles. This research aims to build upon previous findings by examining how topological machine learning can be employed to categorize simple elliptic curves over the complex number field based on their isomorphism relations.

This paper presents a precise QCD prediction for the angular distribution of $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ produced in hadron collisions, incorporating corrections up to next-to-leading order. Focusing on forward rapidity, our calculations yield specific leading-order and next-to-leading-order contributions along with uncertainties, enabling comparisons with experimental data. Moreover, our results reveal notable deviations in the NGN term from both measurements and leading-order predictions. Additionally, this study calculates the anisotropic ALICE parameter $A_{20}$ for forward $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ pairs and finds it to be negative and non-negligible, in line with our earlier findings and experimental outcomes. Our findings support the notion that anisotropic angular distributions arise, likely due to color octurk contributions dominating over color singlet ones at large rapidity values.

We examined 77,313 users who use Signal as their primary messaging platform to understand the underlying factors influencing their key security function, key exchange, behavior. Our research reveals distinct patterns in key exchange behavior between enthusiastic users (n=19) and casual users (n=77), with enthusiastic users actively maintaining their Security Health Checks, regularly updating their PINs, and prioritizing their security over casual users who show little interest in managing their PINs. Notably, our results contradict the common assumption that casual users thoughtfully manage their PINs, with them showing a random approach to PIN updates and little concern for their Security Health Check validations.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products of the Planck and Milne-Eddington distribution functions over wavelength or frequency ranges. By leveraging the smoothness properties of these distribution functions, a new category of quadrature rules has been created, enabling the use of a small number of nodes to achieve exceptional accuracy without requiring repeated computations when parameters change. These rules have been successfully tested against a comprehensive set of parameters, achieving exceptional precision to ten decimal places. By leveraging their accelerated quadrature convergence, highly accurate evaluations of the Planck and Milne-Eddington distribution function product can be achieved, ultimately reducing computational complexity, particularly in large-scale simulations such as radiative transfer modeling, by an order of magnitude. By streamlining calculations of key radiative transfer quantities like emissivity and intensity, as well as vertical radiative flux, the quadrature-based approach yields precise results, all to within four decimal places.

The curvature information contained within the Hessian matrix, or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation $\tilde H = V\Lambda V^T$, or even $V\Lambda^\dagger V^T$, can greatly aid in diagnosing training progress for deep networks. Nevertheless, obtaining and visualizing this information is not straightforward. Our approach leverages the singular value decomposition $[H^{1/2}X^T; 0] = U\Sigma^{1/2}V^T$ to derive a computationally efficient $O(d^2)$ approximation of $\tilde H$, based on optimizing $U\Lambda U^T$ and $UVU^T$. The resulting structure $UVU^T$ is essentially a "square root" approximation of $\tilde H$, allowing us to iteratively estimate the Hessian via Newton iterations. The cost of these iterations is mitigated by employing a Kronecker-based limited memory limited memory Newton (KLLM-Newton) method. The project is hosted at https://github.com/facebookresearch/hessian_flow.

This research investigates how grammatical gender in languages affects the way we classify inanimate objects in the human mind. We focus on word embeddings from multilingual language models and measure their gender-based division in the feature space. We discover that objects with no life have clearly marked feminine and masculine genders. We compare these gender-based divisions with the characteristics of the objects, finding that nouns with feminine genders are more often associated with objects with similar qualities like being weak or artificial. We explore the reasons behind this gendered representation of inanimate objects and suggest that it stems from a combination of factors including historical root patterns, physical characteristics, and social attributes.

We demonstrate a connection between the set of stationary probability measures of non-convex non-contracting maps on the space of n x n real matrices and the concept of stiffness. This relationship reveals that the map's behavior becomes increasingly stable as it does not contract, particularly when considering a non-convex behavior control property. The behavior of a particular class of joint action on n x n real matrices demonstrates how the convergence rate of the resulting stationary measures can be arbitrarily slow, even when no contractive direction is present. The example can be extended to include cases where the convergence rate is irrational multiples of $\pi$. The analysis also extends to non-affine maps, with the requirement that they are uniformly bounded in their second derivative. The connection between stationary measures and dynamics is further explored through its implications on global attractors and chaos theory, highlighting its relevance to a range of phenomena such as laser emission, chemical reactions, pattern formation, and turbulence.

Estimating object poses is a difficult task for new categories without object-specific training. To overcome this problem, we developed a model-driven approach to object pose estimation that leverages object geometry and physical properties. The model selection process starts with a vast database of object geometries and extends to a wide range of object geometries with similar physical properties. To accomplish this, our approach formulates pose estimation as a root-finding problem in a physical state space, where a simulated image derived from the threeD object geometry needs to match the observed twoD image. To resolve the pose estimation problem, we employ the BFGS algorithm, which relies on simulated image differentials with respect to the Euler angles. To ensure our method generalizes well to unseen object geometries, we use differentiable random image augmentation to enhance the robustness of the model. To overcome the computational hurdle of calculating these augmentations, we employed PyTorch's automatic differentiation functionality. To overcome the limitation of insufficient object pose coverage, we employed novel sampling techniques that increase the number of object poses and facilitate learning for unseen object geometries. To overcome the problem of distinguishing pose estimation, we employed random image overlays and found that our model generalizes well to novel object geometries due to the incorporation of object geometry and physical properties. To validate our method, we employed everyday objects from the ShapeNet database and utilized data from the TUM-RGB-D dataset for the everyday object category "monitor". The experiment results show that our method generalizes

This research delves into the creation of a predictive system that synthesizes various models to determine current traffic conditions across entire networks, by first exploring how practitioners approach the selection of feature-engineering methods, then examining available machine learning techniques for extracting these features, and finally examining different models used to calculate traffic state. One essential component of the problem involves identifying the most suitable features through analysis and selection. This process typically occurs in two stages: initially, a set of potential features is manually created, and then, a most effective subset is chosen through additional analysis. Although feature engineering typically relies on human intervention, the application of machine learning could potentially reduce the required time and expertise. Moreover, researchers have identified several other considerations to optimize the overall system, such as the availability of up-to-date data, the availability of suitable computing resources, and the ability to effectively utilize multiple prediction models. This research also examines various real-world approaches to each stage of the traffic state estimation process.

This study presents VCE, a novel method for identifying key variables that enable valid causal effects within a given dataset. We utilize an arbitrary Structural Causal Model to represent the causal relationships underlying the data distribution. Our approach relies on a set of assumptions, specifically back-door path blockages, to ensure accurate causal effect estimation. We formulate this problem as the Causal Variable Cutset Problem, where the goal is to find a set of variables that block all back-door paths between a treatment and outcome, thereby enabling causal effect estimation. This problem is an extension of the classic Variable Cutset Problem and is an NP-hard problem. We develop a linear programming relaxation of the Causal Variable Cutset Problem, providing a lower bound for the optimal solution and guiding the search through a branch-and-bound algorithm. We also introduce a greedy heuristic that provides an approximate solution to this problem. Our method, Causal Variable Cutset, is implemented within the CECI library using Google OR-Tools and demonstrates significant potential in experimental designs that aim to block back-door paths, such as causal-effect estimation in A/B testing, and shows that prior heuristics for blocking back-door paths are unnecessarily conservative.

The number of rare radio phenomena detected is limited due to dependence on large radio interferometers, which are not continuously monitored. We highlight some of these phenomena, such as bursting Reber sources, metamorphosis events, and other transient phenomena that require ongoing monitoring for detection. We discuss the characteristics of modern radio interferometers, like the LOFAR telescope, and evaluate their ability to detect these phenomena. We highlight the advantages of using wide-field, sensitive interferometers like the LOFAR, which can increase the probability of detecting such events by allowing the observation of larger areas of the sky.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to the development of innovative photonic systems and devices. The application of AI/ML methodologies in optics, optoelectronics, and quantum information is set to accelerate in the future. The rapid integration of AI/ML in photonics has fostered a need for comprehensive reviews of AI/ML employed in photonic devices, systems, and applications. This review offers a thorough overview of the underlying principles and state-of-the-art strategies in photonics and machine learning, providing a comprehensive summary of AI/ML-based photonic technologies and their recent progress. Furthermore, we will explore the future challenges and opportunities within the field, as well as the potential for further advancements in AI-driven photonics research.

The research investigates how to create a marketing plan that maximizes a movie's earnings
by analyzing data from 1,746 US releases between 1992 and 2015.  Key factors impacting
this decision include release timing, initial marketing expenditure, ticket pricing, and the
movie's popularity, measured by review scores and audience responses.  Analysis shows that
release timing, marketing spending, and pricing often clash, requiring strategic trade-offs
to optimize a movie's profitability.  Using data, our research identifies the ideal marketing
strategy for each movie, revealing release timing and initial marketing spending significantly
affect revenue.  Notably, higher marketing spending, early release dates, and strategic
marketing during key periods can all contribute to a movie's financial success.  These
findings have practical implications, suggesting early marketing investment is crucial for
a movie's long-term profitability and encouraging strategic marketing planning to maximize
revenue potential.

The power grid's stability hinges on the simultaneous satisfaction of two critical parameters: voltage magnitude and frequency. Although most research focuses on the parameter with the tighter bounds, this paper addresses control strategies for both. Specifically, it investigates the dynamic behavior of damped power systems under random fluctuations in load and renewable energy sources, as well as supply and demand. Stochastic models derived from these interactions exhibit non-rigid critical points, resulting in distinct phase transitions when parameter thresholds are crossed. Building on this framework, the paper presents a first-principles analysis of load-limited load shedding (LLLS) load shedding, focusing on the effects of randomness, system size, and non-rigid phase transitions.

Cyberphysical systems (CPS) are set to see an increase in complexity, spanning multiple domains such as automotive, healthcare, and manufacturing. The shift to connected and highly automated systems will enable a broader adoption of System of Systems (SoS) approaches, which can provide previously unattainable capabilities like self-driving cars, wearable health monitoring, and smart factory automation. The increasing complexity of SoS-based CPS poses significant safety concerns, necessitating a comprehensive approach that encompasses various development and analysis stages. A particular challenge lies in synchronizing cyber and physical components, which could lead to critical consequences such as traffic accidents or life-threatening medical malfunctions. Therefore, a crucial requirement for SoS-based CPS is ensuring safety, which is the focus of this research. Our proposed methodology involves developing a Model-Driven Engineering (MDA) framework that aids in creating a unified, formal model of a SoS-based CPS, allowing for the integration of cyber and physical components and non-functional requirements like security. This approach is demonstrated through its application to two automotive-soS based CPS, namely an emergency braking system and a vehicle platooning system, which are expected to provide a reliable and efficient path to a higher level of security in SoS-based CPS.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions exhibit excess emissions in the ultraviolet and soft X-ray spectrum. To understand the origin of these emissions, it is necessary to differentiate between them as they can have various astrophysical origins. The reflection of blazar light from a thin accretion disk around a black hole is believed to be a potential source of such emissions. The phenomenon of blazar emission reflection, first proposed by Li \& Zdziarski (2013), has been developed to explain visible light and X-ray emissions. Building upon this concept, the authors extend this idea to include gamma rays in the reflection component of blazar emissions, specifically for those with UV/X-ray excess. Two newly developed emission models for the UV/X-ray and gamma-ray components are created, alongside a formula to estimate the amount of scattered gamma-ray emission observed, based on the energy of input photons and the scattering angle. ZK reflection, which involves a cold, black body surface, is also extended to nanogaps - regions with ultra-high electric fields in the accretion disk. ZK reflection in nanogaps - nanoreflection, is shown to produce distinct patterns in the emitted radiation. The phase dependence of the reflected light in blazars with UV/X-ray excess and gamma-ray emissions is investigated, with findings suggesting blazars to have accretion disks with deeper potential wells than Newtonian predictions, based on their observed light curves.

In our study, we investigate the location and behavior of stationary points more thoroughly, particularly focusing on their relationship with saddle points and Stokes rays, which play a significant role in understanding landscape topology. We developed a method to analyze the Hessian matrix at critical points of a complex function and demonstrated its effectiveness through applications to the loss landscape of a neural network trained on a two-dimensional dataset.

In this context, we examine the task of accurately identifying an unknown state from a sequence of related random choices, each influenced by the previous one. Specifically, we focus on distinguishing between two unique states, available repeatedly, with each choice made independently. Our results demonstrate that an online method using all available information can perfectly identify these states, achieving a perfect success rate even as the sequence becomes infinitely long. Surprisingly, this approach outperforms any strategy that only uses the initial information, which may fail in the long run for certain scenarios. Additionally, we extend our analysis to more complex situations involving multiple possible states, showing that an online method can reach the highest possible success rate independently of the sequence's length.

Baryon creation is explored through the process of baryon number transport and the dynamics of string breakups, as predicted by quantum chromodynamics. Baryon yields are evaluated, particularly in terms of the ratio of baryon to meson production, with a focus on its dependence on energy and a comparison to experimental findings. Quantum effects on baryon number fluctuations are examined and results are also compared to measured data. To assess the non-Bose-Gas nature of the string model, ratios of multi-baryon production to multinucleon production are examined and findings are compared to experimental evidence.

In this study, we are investigating whether the fluctuations of helioseismic data along the Sun's surface are influenced by solar activity cycles. Previous research has proposed explanations based on changes in sound speed, but the role of mass movements, like those caused by the dynamic movement of solar activity, remains unclear. In this work, we've developed a mathematical model that accounts of both changes in sound speed, and mass movements, and how solar activity affects the data. We've found that the data is a combination of these two factors, and that mass movements, like those caused by solar activity, can fully explain the changes in the data over the solar activity cycles. In order to verify this, we've used advanced computer simulations to study how solar activity affects the movement of mass around solar areas, and whether these movements are strong enough to have a significant effect on the data and the data's response to sound speed changes. Our results show that the computer simulations agree with the findings of a one-dimensional model, suggesting that the changes in the data can be fully explained by mass movements, and that sound speed changes in the data are a more intricate process, and need further investigation.

We have proposed an alternative explanation for the origin of gravitational waves in the early universe, attributing them to the turbulent motion of energy within it. This novel perspective is grounded in an unusual phenomenon where dark matter interacts with standard matter through a connection that weakens with increasing distance, which also accounts for the observed missing gravitational effects of galaxy cluster material. This unique setup enables us to propose that gravitational waves form a background due to turbulent motion, possibly generated by sudden changes in particle phenomena, where energy is transferred between different scales, ultimately leading to turbulence, which may have occurred shortly after the universe began, when it was in a hot, quark-gluon plasma state, and where gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years later, when the universe's age was approximately 100 million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may have ultimately led to gravitational wave background may have formed a century million years, which may

Light field imaging offers increased flexibility in focusing, perspective, and exposure, but face-on-demand resolution remains a significant challenge due to the trade-off between image quality and available memory bandwidth. The main issue lies in the high memory traffic required to reconstruct high-resolution views from multiple light field rays, particularly when applying computationally intensive image processing techniques, such as advanced denoising methods. In response to this challenge, researchers have developed a new Non-local Means style denoising algorithm, specifically designed to meet the constraints of light field processors, including the available memory bandwidth and cache capacity. The effectiveness of this approach has been tested with real light field data, and the results indicate that it meets memory traffic requirements while producing high-quality denoised views that are indistinguishable from those produced by methods with unlimited memory resources, and outperforms existing methods with requirements similar to those of light field processors.

In this study, we investigate two typical approaches to vector-based cross-lingual search: the initialization of zero-shot search with pre-trained language models (PLMs) and the creation of a supervised dual-encoder framework. We find that the quality of supervised search is contingent upon the relevance of training parallel sentence pairs to query-document pairs. To enhance vector-quality bilingual pairs, we develop a pre-training task rooted in the principles of previous cross-sentence pre-training work and three relevant theses. The proposed task, named XLCLoPP, simulates cross-lingual sentence-sentence retrieval. We then generate large quantities of relevant cross-lingual pairs from target-source documents and use them to develop a cross-lingual similarity space through CL retrieval pre-training. We evaluate the generated bilingual embeddings across three datasets under both single-view and cross-view scenarios and demonstrate their efficacy surpassing existing approaches. We openly share all our models and code for future research purposes.

The way public health policies shape the lives of people across the globe, making it crucial for the field of Demography to understand the interplay between these policies and the characteristics of the populations they affect. However, data collection in this field often involves a significant challenge - the need to consider the underlying design of the surveys or censuses when performing demographic analyses. Although this issue has been well-documented in statistical literature, it has been largely overlooked in the field of Demography. Our research focuses on a case study involving a CDC public health policy policy (the National Cancer Institute's Breast and Cervical Cancer Prevention and Control Program) that targets specific low-income counties across the US. By treating the policy's implementation as an experimental treatment affecting the treatment counties and comparing them to non-treatment states, we demonstrate how a demographic analysis can be informed by an approach that considers the underlying sampling design of the data collected across the states. Our analysis uses a framework that combines the features of post-stratification, weights, and small area demographics to account for the underlying sampling design in our analysis. Our results show that when considering the underlying sampling design, the demographic estimates of the treated counties reveal a more accurate picture of the impact of the policy than traditional methods. Our study highlights the potential for a more nuanced understanding of the impact of public health policies by taking the underlying sampling design into account, and it provides specific recommendations for the field of Demography to consider the underlying sampling design in their analyses.

The theoretical framework of thermodynamic betting has been established to explore the fundamental limits of knowledge through the lens of resource theory. In this approach, the act of investing energy in a unitary process is seen as equivalent to betting capital on the system's outcome, with "house profit" defined by the energy cost in relation to the assigned probabilities. Distinguishable from traditional quantum betting models, this concept relies on the dynamical evolution of states rather than prior distributions, highlighting the inherent trade-offs involved. Notably, this formalism has a direct connection to quantum thermodynamics, where the energy can be reinterpreted as a form of betting capital.

Building on the recently developed two-dimensional hybrid functional method for
efficiently handling van der Waals interactions, we have developed a hybrid
approinxHF-DFT method that combines quantum Monte Carlo and density functional
theory to calculate the band alignment of 2D materials. Using this method, we
have applied it to a series of transition metal dichalcogenides, comparing the
results with experimental data to show good quasiparticle band gap agreement.
Additionally, we have used HF-DFT to study the band alignment in graphene, MoS2,
and a series of silicene and antimonene polymorphs, demonstrating its utility in
the absence of reliable experimental data for these 2D materials.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Observations of the broad-band continuum and spectral lines from protoplanetary disks have shown that their inner, dense regions exhibit brighter emissions than predicted by standard models. This discrepancy suggests that an inward flow of disk material is occurring, which could have a significant impact on the formation of planetary systems. This phenomenon is examined through the influence of material transport on spectral line emissions, with a focus on the effects of a flow-driven model compared to static models. It has been demonstrated that a modest flow rate of approximately 10^-3 times the Earth's mass per million years is sufficient to explain this enhanced emission by about 20 percent. Moreover, this level of mass transport could significantly affect the distribution of dust within the disk, thereby impacting the formation of planets.

Astronomical observations from the ground are compromised by atmospheric dispersion, a phenomenon that significantly affects the accuracy of measured properties like color and metallicity of stars. To counteract this, observations often utilize Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors (ADCs) but despite their use, uncertainties in these measurements remain. The following paper details our development of a method to precisely quantify the performance of ADCs in real-time, a innovation enabled by machine learning. By integrating observations of artificial dispersion sources across various wavelengths, this method accurately predicts the effectiveness of the ADC along with atmospheric dispersion, all with a high degree of accuracy.

This paper proposes a novel hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibits inherent trend homogeneity across different periods. We establish a straightforward method for generating observations from our proposed model and introduce an empirical Bayes approach to identify optimal parameter values. To handle temporal homogeneity, we utilize an empirical T\`{o}ker\`{u} prior, yielding an efficient empirical null distribution for variance-covariance matrices and a corresponding initial estimator of the model's parameters. We then develop a maximum likelihood estimation procedure to refine initial estimates and obtain optimal parameter values over time. To analyze the model, we investigate its basic properties and the asymptotic behavior of the refined estimators. We further evaluate the model through a simulation study and apply it to a real-world application: a hierarchical latent variable model to track the spread of COVID-19 across multiple periods. We propose a novel maximum likelihood estimation procedure for a novel hierarchical latent variable model to capture trends in multi-period time series data, and use it to monitor the spread of COVID-19 over multiple periods. We establish a simple method to generate observations from our proposed model and introduce an efficient approach to identify optimal parameter values. We handle temporal homogeneity using the empirical T\`{o}ker\`{u} prior, along with corresponding null distributions and initial estimators of the model's parameters.
